meta.blurb: Odile opens her new flat and finds a stranger inside, holding a key to the same door. The agent booked it twice, and nothing else is free for a month. One violin, one microphone, one strip of tape.
meta.bible: Odile Brandt: 31, a violin teacher, tidy and careful, secretly lost her place in the city orchestra and has not told her family; practises every afternoon. Sam Ferreira: 30, a sound engineer who works from home with headphones and cables, untidy, kind, bad at saying what he feels; fears his small studio will fail. Ms Vane: the letting agent at Vane and Co, who double-booked the flat. Mr Quill: the landlord, away abroad, returns late. Mrs Okonkwo: the elderly neighbour in Flat 3B, wise and funny, owner of the cat Biscuit, about to move to live near her daughter. Biscuit: the grey cat who escapes. Tilly: 9, Odile's pupil, shy, plays the violin. Dev: Sam's best friend, a cheerful cook. Mrs Brandt: Odile's mother, Hélène Brandt, who visits for a weekend. Lamplighter Lane: the street. Flat 4B: the top-floor flat, one bedroom, a tiny study with a sofa, a long hall, a noisy kitchen, a stairwell with a beautiful echo. Flat 3B: the flat below, with high ceilings and a big front room. Corn Hall: where Tilly's recital is held. Larkspur Children's Choir: the choir Sam records. Stairwell Songs: the album they make, recorded in the echoing stairwell at midnight. The tape line: a strip of blue masking tape down the hall that divides the flat. Ending: Mr Quill leases Flat 3B to Odile and Sam together; they carry their boxes down one floor and try both keys in the same door. Voice and tone: warm, funny, gentle, slow-burning; a home, a sound and a friendship that becomes love; clean, no bad language. More facts: Winnie: the ribbon microphone Sam names and talks to. Mr Tavish: the grumpy retired postman in Flat 2A, who dislikes noise and later loves the choir. Ms Pereira: the director of the Larkspur Children's Choir, brisk and warm. Mr and Mrs Marsh: Tilly's parents. Mr Halloran: the conductor of the City Orchestra, who held the yearly re-audition where Odile's nerves froze her bow and she lost her chair. Grandpa Luc: Odile's late grandfather, who gave her the violin. Arlo: a small choir boy who sings loudly and off key and wins everyone over. Ngozi: Mrs Okonkwo's daughter, who lives by the sea. Odile and Sam share the rent, halved by Ms Vane as an apology. A sock on the bathroom door handle means occupied. Sam's equipment loan is his fear. The album is due at the end of the month and is delivered the Friday before Tilly's Saturday recital. Tilly's full name is Tilly Marsh. Harbour Road and Kiln Street: the two other flats Ms Vane finds, on opposite sides of the city; Odile's would be on Harbour Road, Sam's on Kiln Street. Mr Tavish spends weekends at his sister's by the river. When Mrs Okonkwo moves to the sea, Biscuit escapes his basket and stays with Odile and Sam. Flat 3B has two bedrooms, a big sunlit front room and an old piano that stays. Mr Quill writes the lease with both their names. The album is released in the autumn; Odile plays the first note and teaches the choir; Sam's studio is saved.
chapters: Say It Before It Is Too Late

beats.scene: A young woman climbs narrow stairs with a suitcase and a violin case
beats.summary: Odile Brandt climbs the four flights of 22 Lamplighter Lane with her suitcase, her violin and the key to Flat 4B.

beats.scene: A grey cat watches from a half-open door on the third floor landing
beats.summary: On the third landing a grey cat watches her from a half-open door, and an old voice says the top flat has a lovely echo.

beats.scene: A woman pauses at a front door holding a violin case and a key
beats.summary: At the door of 4B she hopes this quiet flat will let her start again, though she has told nobody why she needed a fresh start.

beats.scene: A man in large headphones stands among boxes holding a key
beats.summary: She opens the door and finds Sam Ferreira already inside, in headphones, holding a key exactly like hers.

beats.scene: The man jumps and pulls off his headphones as the woman points at him
beats.summary: Sam jumps, drops a cable and says she must have the wrong flat, because this is his.

beats.scene: Two strangers hold up crumpled papers at a kitchen counter
beats.summary: They introduce themselves and lay their rental papers side by side: both are for Flat 4B and both begin today.

beats.scene: Two keys are tried in the same lock of a front door
beats.summary: To be sure, each tries their key in the door, and both keys turn the same lock.

beats.scene: A man holds a phone on speaker while a woman listens with folded arms
beats.summary: They ring Ms Vane at the letting agency, who says in a rush that the flat was booked twice by mistake.

beats.scene: A woman scrolls a list on a phone while a man shakes his head
beats.summary: Ms Vane checks her list and says nothing else is free for a month, because the city is full for a big festival.

beats.scene: A woman sits on a suitcase beside a man leaning on a wall
beats.summary: Odile's old flat has been sold and Sam's lease has ended, and both have already paid their deposits.

beats.scene: A man scrolls his phone beside a woman making a call on a staircase
beats.summary: Both try other ways out: Odile rings a friend who is away, and Sam's friend Dev has a full house.

beats.scene: A woman frowns at a phone showing hotel prices
beats.summary: Odile checks hotels on her phone and finds every price far above what a teacher can pay for a whole month.

beats.scene: A tall man spreads his hands while a woman stares at him in horror
beats.summary: Sam suggests the plain answer: they share the flat for the month, and Odile is horrified.

beats.scene: A woman looks at a tall pile of cables and microphones
beats.summary: Odile points to his cables, boxes and microphones and says she has never lived with a man who owns so many wires.

beats.scene: A woman walks toward the front door with her suitcase and stops
beats.summary: Odile picks up her suitcase to leave, looks at the four flights of stairs and has nowhere to go.

beats.scene: Two people sit at a counter with a phone between them and a paper
beats.summary: Ms Vane rings back and offers each of them half the rent for the month, as a way to say sorry.

beats.scene: A long hall with doors, and a tiny study with a sofa
beats.summary: They walk round the flat: a long hall, a noisy kitchen, one bedroom and a tiny study with a short sofa.

beats.scene: A man and a woman stand on either side of a bedroom doorway
beats.summary: Both want the one bedroom: Odile for her violin and her peace, Sam because the sofa would never fit him.

beats.scene: A coin spins in the air above two open hands
beats.summary: They agree to toss a coin: Odile calls heads, the coin spins in the air, and the whole flat seems to hold its breath.

beats.scene: A tall man lies on a tiny sofa, feet over the end
beats.summary: The coin says heads: Odile takes the bedroom, and Sam folds himself onto the short sofa in the study and names his microphone Winnie.

beats.scene: A woman sits on a bed and opens a violin case
beats.summary: In her new room Odile sits on the bed, opens her violin case and promises herself she will practise every day.

beats.scene: A man sits on a kitchen counter eating cold toast
beats.summary: In the kitchen they find one kettle, two mugs and a loaf of bread, and they begin to argue about whose shelf is whose.

beats.scene: A man comes through the door holding a roll of blue tape
beats.summary: Sam goes out to the shop and comes back with a roll of blue masking tape and a plan.

beats.scene: A man kneels in a long hall pressing blue tape onto the wooden floor
beats.summary: Sam presses a line of tape down the middle of the long hall, then across the front room, to divide the flat in two.

beats.scene: A woman points at a bathroom door beside a blue tape line
beats.summary: Odile points out that the bathroom is on her side, and they agree that a sock on the door handle will mean someone is inside.

beats.scene: Two people label shelves in an open fridge with strips of tape
beats.summary: They split the cupboards and the fridge: top shelf for Odile, bottom shelf for Sam, and one pan each.

beats.scene: Two people eat at opposite ends of a long table
beats.summary: They eat separately that night: Odile has plain pasta, Sam has beans on toast, and they sit at opposite ends of the table.

beats.scene: A woman tunes a violin by a window as the evening light fades
beats.summary: The afternoon was lost to the move, so at seven Odile begins her practice, starting with long, slow scales.

beats.scene: A man in headphones glares at the wall above his desk
beats.summary: In the study, Sam is trying to record and hears the scales through the wall, and the take is ruined.

beats.scene: A man bangs on a wall as a woman shouts back
beats.summary: Sam knocks on the wall, then calls out politely, then less politely, and Odile answers that she must practise.

beats.scene: A woman lowers her violin as the room falls quiet at nine o'clock
beats.summary: At nine Odile stops playing, and the flat goes quiet except for the pipes, which tap like a drummer in the wall.

beats.scene: A woman lies awake in bed while a faint light shines under the door
beats.summary: In the dark she hears Sam laughing at his own recordings through the wall, and it keeps her awake.

beats.scene: A man hums to himself at a desk covered in blinking lights
beats.summary: At midnight she still cannot sleep; she listens to Sam hum along to a goose honking on a tape, and the sound is oddly kind.

beats.scene: A yawning woman waits by a bathroom door with a sock on it
beats.summary: In the morning they both want the bathroom, and Odile finds Sam's sock on the handle and waits, yawning, in the hall.

beats.scene: A man and a woman wait for one kettle, each holding a mug
beats.summary: In the kitchen there is only one kettle, and Odile and Sam stand with their mugs, each waiting for the other to move.

beats.scene: A man and a woman write a timetable on paper at a kitchen counter
beats.summary: They agree they need rules: Odile may play from four to six, and Sam will record only after nine.

beats.scene: A paper timetable under a magnet on a fridge door
beats.summary: The timetable goes onto the fridge under a magnet, and Sam adds a small note at the bottom that says no scales before breakfast.

beats.scene: A paper note on the fridge in two different handwritings
beats.summary: Notes begin to appear: Sam asks her to stop moving his pan, and Odile writes back that a pan is not a pet.

beats.scene: A fridge covered in notes about socks and a dirty pan
beats.summary: The notes grow snippy: one about socks on the radiator, one about a dirty pan left overnight, and one that says please read the timetable.

beats.scene: A drawn violin and a microphone with a moustache on a note
beats.summary: Odile draws a tiny violin on a note, and Sam answers with a microphone wearing a moustache, and she hides her smile.

beats.scene: A grey cat leaps through an open window into a sunny room
beats.summary: On the fourth afternoon, as Odile plays, a grey cat leaps through the open window and lands on Sam's desk.

beats.scene: A man grabs at a grey cat that jumps over a pile of boxes
beats.summary: Sam tries to catch the cat, but it leaps from the desk and runs off down the hall, knocking over a stack of boxes.

beats.scene: A man and a woman crawl on the floor looking under a sofa
beats.summary: The cat hides under the sofa, and Odile and Sam crawl across the tape line from both sides to catch it.

beats.scene: A grey cat sits on a violin case while two people hold their breath
beats.summary: The cat strolls out and sits down on Odile's violin case, and both of them freeze, afraid to scare it.

beats.scene: An old woman in a green cardigan stands at a door
beats.summary: A knock at the door: Mrs Okonkwo from Flat 3B has come for her cat, and says Biscuit loves visiting the top flat.

beats.scene: An old woman holds a cat and smiles at two people on the floor
beats.summary: Mrs Okonkwo lifts Biscuit, looks at them on the floor with torches, and says they make a lovely noise together.

beats.scene: An old woman peers at a blue tape line on a hallway floor
beats.summary: Mrs Okonkwo notices the blue tape, raises her eyebrows, and invites them both to tea on Thursday.

beats.scene: An old woman pours tea in a high-ceilinged room with a dusty piano
beats.summary: On Thursday, tea in Flat 3B: high ceilings, a big front room, a dusty piano and photographs of Mrs Okonkwo's daughter by the sea.

beats.scene: An old woman and two guests sit with teacups beside a piano
beats.summary: Mrs Okonkwo says her daughter wants her to move to the coast, and she is slowly thinking about it, though she loves this building.

beats.scene: A woman plays violin in a high room as a man listens
beats.summary: Mrs Okonkwo asks Odile to play, and after a moment she does; Sam listens from the doorway, very still.

beats.scene: A woman folds a letter and puts it at the bottom of a drawer
beats.summary: That night Odile takes out a letter from the City Orchestra and folds it into a drawer: she has lost her chair, and nobody at home knows.

beats.scene: A man dances around a kitchen holding a phone and a calendar
beats.summary: Next morning Sam gets a phone call: the Larkspur Children's Choir has chosen him, and he circles a date four weeks away on the calendar.

beats.scene: A man shows a woman a calendar with one date circled
beats.summary: Sam tells Odile at the fridge, and she says sincerely that he must be very proud, though he looks a little pale.

beats.scene: A man draws a plan of eight songs on a large sheet of paper
beats.summary: Sam explains the plan: eight songs, forty children, three weekends of recording, and one quiet, perfect room.

beats.scene: A man holds a microphone in a quiet study with the window open
beats.summary: He tests the study first: through the walls come traffic, the fridge hum and the knocking of the pipes.

beats.scene: A man carries a microphone through a kitchen, a hall and a bathroom
beats.summary: He carries Winnie through the whole flat: the kitchen is full of kettle noise, the hall is flat, and the bathroom echoes too much.

beats.scene: A man sits on the floor among cables with his head in his hands
beats.summary: Back in the study he sits among his cables, tired and worried, and he throws his headphones onto the sofa.

beats.scene: A woman stops playing and rests her violin on her knee in a bedroom
beats.summary: In the afternoon Odile begins her hour, but her bow shakes and she stops in the middle of a phrase; the flat grows silent.

beats.scene: A man types on a phone while a pot sits on a stove
beats.summary: Sam, hearing the silence, texts his friend Dev for a simple recipe, and Dev answers with seven messages.

beats.scene: A man stirs a pot while smoke rises from a second burned pot
beats.summary: Sam burns the first pot, rescues the second, and when the soup is good, he carries it into the hall.

beats.scene: A pot of soup sits on a blue tape line with a handwritten note
beats.summary: Sam sets the pot of soup on the tape line and tapes a note to the lid that says soup may cross the tape.

beats.scene: A woman stands in a doorway looking down at a pot of soup
beats.summary: Odile finds the pot, reads the note, and wonders whether to accept it, because she dislikes owing anyone a favour.

beats.scene: A woman tastes soup from a spoon with surprised eyes
beats.summary: She takes a spoonful, and the soup is excellent, so she eats two bowls standing up in the kitchen.

beats.scene: A woman writes on a sticky note with a pen above a washed bowl
beats.summary: She washes the bowl and writes a note: soup approved, and would he like to hear Bach at six?

beats.scene: A man reads a note at a study door and stares at the clock
beats.summary: Sam reads the note, wonders if he is being invited or only warned, and at two minutes to six he takes off his headphones.

beats.scene: A woman plays violin in a long hall, a man on the floor
beats.summary: At six Odile plays Bach in the hall, and Sam sits on the floor on his side of the tape and listens without a word.

beats.scene: A man stands up as a woman lowers her violin
beats.summary: When she finishes, Sam says only thank you, goes back to the study, and plays nothing at all for an hour.

beats.scene: A small girl with a violin stands beside her teacher
beats.summary: The next day Odile's pupil Tilly, aged nine, arrives with her father for a lesson in the front room.

beats.scene: A man at a study door holds a stub of chalk
beats.summary: Sam hides in the study during the lesson, but when he hears a peg slip out of tune, he comes out with a tip.

beats.scene: A shy girl with a violin smiles up at a man
beats.summary: The chalk works, Tilly smiles for the first time, and then asks Odile whether Sam is her husband.

beats.scene: A man with a bag of bottles stops on a stair landing
beats.summary: Next evening Sam carries the recycling downstairs, drops a spoon on the stone steps, and stops to listen to the ring.

beats.scene: A man claps his hands on a stairwell landing under a round window
beats.summary: He claps once and hears a long, rich echo, and he runs up and down every flight of stairs testing each landing.

beats.scene: A man talks excitedly at a kitchen door while a woman folds her arms
beats.summary: He bursts into the flat and tells Odile excitedly that the stairwell is the perfect place to record, but she is not sure.

beats.scene: A woman plays a violin on a stair landing
beats.summary: On the landing Odile plays a single long note, and it blooms around them, and she stops, surprised.

beats.scene: An old woman leans out of a door on the third floor landing smiling
beats.summary: Mrs Okonkwo leans out of her door below and says the old choir used to sing on those stairs at Christmas, years ago.

beats.scene: A man in a dressing gown glares up from a second floor landing
beats.summary: Mr Tavish from Flat 2A comes out in a dressing gown and says the stairs are for walking, not for concerts.

beats.scene: A man hangs a microphone on a string from a stair banister
beats.summary: At midnight, when Mr Tavish is away at his sister's, Sam hangs Winnie from the banister on a string and runs cables down the stairs.

beats.scene: A woman in a coat over pyjamas plays violin on a dark landing
beats.summary: Odile comes out in a coat over her pyjamas to test the sound, and plays a few quiet notes while Sam presses record.

beats.scene: A man listens through headphones with wide eyes and a woman waits
beats.summary: Sam plays back the recording and his eyes go wide, and he hands her the headphones without a word.

beats.scene: A woman wearing headphones looks up at a man who is smiling
beats.summary: Odile hears her violin, free and warm and unhurried, and Sam tells her quietly that she is not only a teacher.

beats.scene: Two people sit on a dark stair landing with two mugs of tea
beats.summary: The next night Sam brings two mugs of tea to the landing, and they sit on the steps with the microphone asleep between them.

beats.scene: A woman with her knees drawn up speaks quietly on a staircase
beats.summary: Odile tells him she played for six years in the City Orchestra, and that this spring she lost her chair.

beats.scene: A conductor raises a baton in an empty hall before a nervous violinist
beats.summary: She describes the yearly audition: Mr Halloran, the conductor, sat in the dark hall, and she began to play.

beats.scene: A violinist freezes on an empty stage with her bow trembling
beats.summary: Then her right arm began to shake, the sound broke, and she could not play a single clean bar until the end.

beats.scene: A woman looks at her own hands on a staircase at night
beats.summary: She admits she has told no one, not even her mother, who tells everyone back home that her daughter is in the orchestra.

beats.scene: A man looks gently at a woman as they sit on stairs
beats.summary: Sam does not try to fix it; he only says that a chair is not a violin, and that the violin on the stairs was still hers.

beats.scene: A man rubs his neck and looks at his shoes on stairs
beats.summary: In return Sam admits his own fear: if the choir album fails, his small studio fails, and he has no other plan.

beats.scene: Two people share biscuits on a dark staircase
beats.summary: They share a packet of biscuits, and soon Biscuit the cat arrives up the stairs and sits between them as though he had been invited.

beats.scene: Two handwritten notes on a fridge beside two mugs
beats.summary: In the morning they feel shy about all they said, but the fridge notes are kinder now: tea, yes please.

beats.scene: A worried woman holds a phone to her ear
beats.summary: Odile's mother phones to say she will come for the weekend and hopes to go with Odile to an orchestra concert.

beats.scene: A man holds a vacuum cleaner and a mug beside a worried woman
beats.summary: Sam overheard the call and says he is not offering to fix anything, only tea and a vacuum cleaner, and Odile accepts.

beats.scene: Two people sweep, wipe and tidy a flat full of cables and boxes
beats.summary: They clean the flat from top to bottom, hide Sam's cables in the study and argue about whether to peel up the blue tape.

beats.scene: A small elegant woman with a basket stands on a staircase landing
beats.summary: On Friday evening Mrs Brandt climbs the stairs with a basket of cheese, plum jam and a cake tin, and kisses her daughter on both cheeks.

beats.scene: A mother raises an eyebrow as a tall man shakes her hand
beats.summary: Odile introduces Sam as her flatmate, and her mother's eyebrows rise slowly when she hears there is only one bedroom.

beats.scene: A man cooks at a stove as a woman sniffs the air
beats.summary: Sam cooks dinner for three with Dev's best recipe, and Mrs Brandt eats two plates and asks for the secret.

beats.scene: A mother whispers to a daughter beside a sink full of plates
beats.summary: In the kitchen her mother whispers that Sam is lovely, and Odile whispers back that he is only a flatmate.

beats.scene: A tall man sleeps on an air bed beside a tape line
beats.summary: Mrs Brandt takes the bedroom, Odile takes the sofa in the study, and Sam sleeps on an air bed in the hall beside the tape.

beats.scene: A mother and daughter drink coffee at a kitchen table in morning light
beats.summary: On Saturday morning her mother asks which night the orchestra plays, and Odile puts down her cup and says she has something to tell her.

beats.scene: A woman speaks earnestly across a table while her mother listens
beats.summary: Odile tells her mother the whole truth: the audition, the frozen bow, the letter and the months of silence.

beats.scene: A mother hugs a daughter tightly in a sunny kitchen
beats.summary: Her mother is silent, then hugs her tight and says she is proud of her teaching, and that Grandpa Luc played at weddings and was happy.

beats.scene: A mother kisses her daughter at a door beside two keys
beats.summary: On Sunday Mrs Brandt leaves, tells Sam to keep Odile practising, and notices two keys on one hook by the door.

beats.scene: A woman and a man stand at a counter reading a to-do list
beats.summary: On Monday Odile says she is glad she told the truth, and offers to help with the choir, because she knows how to handle children.

beats.scene: A brisk woman with a clipboard claps her hands on a stairwell landing
beats.summary: Ms Pereira, the choir director, inspects the stairwell with a clipboard, claps once, and says it will do beautifully.

beats.scene: Forty children in coats and scarves line up on the steps of a stairwell
beats.summary: On Saturday forty children in coats and scarves line up on the steps, whispering, giggling and pushing, while Sam places his microphones.

beats.scene: A woman shows a row of children how to stand and breathe
beats.summary: Odile shows the children how to stand tall and breathe from their stomachs, and the noise slowly dies away.

beats.scene: A small boy with a missing front tooth sings loudly with his chin up
beats.summary: The smallest boy, Arlo, sings loudest and most off key, and Odile quietly kneels beside him and shows him how to listen.

beats.scene: A man holds up one hand for silence as children giggle on the stairs
beats.summary: The first takes go wrong: a cough, a sneeze, a passing lorry, and then Biscuit strolls down through the middle of the choir.

beats.scene: A grey-haired man in a dressing gown stands on a stair landing listening
beats.summary: In the middle of a lullaby Mr Tavish returns from his sister's early, appears in his dressing gown, and the children's singing makes him stop.

beats.scene: An old man in a dressing gown listens on a stair
beats.summary: Mr Tavish sits down on the stairs and listens to the end, folding his arms, and when they finish he asks if there is a second verse.

beats.scene: A man holds up two thumbs as children cheer
beats.summary: They record the whole lullaby in three takes; the last is perfect, the children clap, and Sam holds up his thumbs.

beats.scene: A cheerful man carries a huge pot up a staircase
beats.summary: On Sunday Dev arrives with a giant pot and four bags of shopping, announces that he will cook, and spots the blue tape.

beats.scene: A man in an apron points a wooden spoon at a tall man
beats.summary: Dev takes over the kitchen, orders Sam about with a wooden spoon, and says Sam has mentioned Odile at least forty times this week.

beats.scene: Three friends laugh around a table covered with steaming dishes
beats.summary: Over dinner Dev tells embarrassing stories, including the day Sam cried at a whale recording, and Odile laughs until she cannot breathe.

beats.scene: A woman plays violin in a front room while a man watches her face
beats.summary: After dinner Odile plays a short, bright piece, and Dev notices that Sam does not look at the violin at all, only at her.

beats.scene: A man and a woman wash dishes side by side at a sink
beats.summary: At the sink Dev tells Odile that Sam is the kindest man he knows and the worst at saying what he feels.

beats.scene: A cheerful man whispers to a tall man at a front door at night
beats.summary: At the door Dev whispers to Sam to say it before the month ends, and Sam says he has no idea what he means.

beats.scene: A woman in a blazer speaks into a phone in a bright office
beats.summary: On Monday Ms Vane rings with news: two flats are ready, and they must both move out by the end of the week.

beats.scene: Two people smile too widely at each other across a hallway
beats.summary: Both of them say that is great news, too brightly, and neither of them means it.

beats.scene: A man sits at a desk in headphones while a woman plays slowly nearby
beats.summary: That day they avoid each other: Sam works late behind his headphones, and Odile practises Bach slowly, as if every note might be the last.

beats.scene: Two hands tap a thin wall from opposite sides in the dark
beats.summary: That night they lie awake on either side of the wall, and Odile taps twice; after a moment, Sam taps back twice.

beats.scene: A woman reads a message on a phone at a kitchen window
beats.summary: On Wednesday Dev sends Odile a message: it is Sam's birthday tomorrow, and Sam has told nobody.

beats.scene: A woman carries shopping bags of flour and eggs up a staircase
beats.summary: Odile decides to bake him a cake, though she has never baked one, and buys flour, eggs, butter and three candles.

beats.scene: A kitchen covered in flour with a woman holding a whisk
beats.summary: On his birthday morning, while Sam is at a meeting with Ms Pereira, Odile fills the kitchen with flour, steam and a great deal of noise.

beats.scene: A lopsided cake with a sunken middle cooling on a kitchen table
beats.summary: The cake comes out lopsided and sunken in the middle, and when Odile tastes a crumb, it is dreadful, because she used salt in place of sugar.

beats.scene: An old woman in a green cardigan comforts a sad woman in a kitchen
beats.summary: Mrs Okonkwo, who has smelled smoke, climbs the stairs with Biscuit and says that a cake need not be good to be loved.

beats.scene: A man stands in a kitchen doorway looking at a floury mess
beats.summary: Sam comes home early, because the meeting ended well, and stops in the doorway at the sight of the flour and the lopsided cake.

beats.scene: A woman lights three candles on a lopsided cake as a man watches
beats.summary: Odile lights the three candles with trembling hands and says, with a very red face, that it is for his birthday and that it is probably awful.

beats.scene: A man eats a slice of cake while pulling a brave face
beats.summary: Sam takes a large bite, chews for a long time with a fixed smile, and says it is the best cake anyone has ever baked for him.

beats.scene: A woman plays a birthday tune on a violin in a kitchen
beats.summary: To make up for the cake she plays Happy Birthday on the violin, slowly and beautifully, as if it were a piece by Bach.

beats.scene: A man gives a woman a small envelope with a handwritten label
beats.summary: Sam, who had nothing to give her in return, hands her a small drive in an envelope, labelled Not Only A Teacher; it holds her first recording from the stairs.

beats.scene: Two people dance in a small kitchen with music from a phone
beats.summary: That evening, with music from her phone, they dance clumsily around the kitchen, and the line of blue tape is under their feet.

beats.scene: Two people kneel on a hall floor peeling up a long blue tape line
beats.summary: In a sudden rush Sam suggests they take up the tape, and together they peel it off the floor, rolling it into one large blue ball.

beats.scene: A blue ball of tape sits beside a lemon magnet
beats.summary: Odile puts the ball of tape on the kitchen shelf beside the lemon magnet, and says, with a straight face, that it should go in a museum.

beats.scene: Heavy rain streaks a dark window beside a roof
beats.summary: That night a great storm arrives, with thunder, and the rain begins to drum on the roof above the top flat.

beats.scene: A woman in pyjamas stares at a drip falling from a ceiling
beats.summary: In the middle of the night Odile hears a new sound, a drip, and she follows it into the study and sees water falling from the ceiling.

beats.scene: A woman throws a coat over a hard drive as water drips from above
beats.summary: On the desk sits the hard drive that holds the whole choir album, so Odile throws her coat over it and shouts for Sam.

beats.scene: A man in pyjamas lifts a hard drive from a desk
beats.summary: Sam bursts in, half asleep, lifts the hard drive and laptop away from the water and carries them to dry shelves in the hall.

beats.scene: Two people place bowls and pans under a dripping ceiling at night
beats.summary: They put every bowl and pan under the drips and call the number for emergencies at Vane and Co, which rings and rings.

beats.scene: A grumpy man in a dressing gown carries a ladder up a stairwell
beats.summary: Mr Tavish appears at the door in his dressing gown with a ladder and a sheet of plastic, says he carried post through worse, and fixes the leak.

beats.scene: A man and a woman sit on a bed holding a hard drive
beats.summary: When the water stops, they sit side by side on the bed, holding the dry hard drive, and Sam says quietly that the album is safe.

beats.scene: Two people hug on a bed under a wall clock
beats.summary: Their hug goes on a little too long; neither of them moves, and the clock ticks, until Odile says a shy goodnight.

beats.scene: A man copies files from a hard drive to a laptop at dawn
beats.summary: At dawn Sam copies the album three times, onto the laptop, a second drive and a small stick that he drops into Odile's violin case for safety.

beats.scene: A bright woman in a blazer holds two small envelopes at a door
beats.summary: In the morning Ms Vane arrives with two new keys in two envelopes: Odile's flat is on Harbour Road, Sam's on Kiln Street, on opposite sides of the city.

beats.scene: Two hands take two sets of keys from a woman in a blazer
beats.summary: They each take a key without a word, and Ms Vane, puzzled, looks at the ceiling stain and promises a roofer.

beats.scene: A man and a woman pack boxes in silence in a living room
beats.summary: They pack their boxes in silence: Sam wraps and labels his cables one by one, and Odile folds her clothes into neat squares.

beats.scene: A woman folds notes from a fridge door into a violin case
beats.summary: Odile takes down the notes from the fridge, every snippy one and every funny one, and folds them carefully into her violin case with the lemon magnet.

beats.scene: A bare room with boxes and a single microphone on the floor
beats.summary: By evening the flat is empty and echoing, and the sound of every footstep comes back as if the rooms are sad too.

beats.scene: An old woman pours strong tea for a young woman
beats.summary: Mrs Okonkwo invites Odile down for tea and tells her she has decided to move to the sea to live with Ngozi.

beats.scene: An old woman raises her eyebrows at a young woman
beats.summary: Then she adds that she thinks Odile and Sam are two very foolish people who cannot see what is under their own noses.

beats.scene: A woman stands outside a closed study door listening to a quiet voice
beats.summary: Odile climbs the stairs and hears Sam, alone in the empty study, saying quietly to Winnie that he does not want to go.

beats.scene: Two friends talk across a small café table with plates between them
beats.summary: Dev meets Sam at a café, pushes a plate of cake toward him and tells him to say what he feels before it is too late.

beats.scene: A man looks at a napkin covered with crossed-out words
beats.summary: Sam says that Odile has a violin, a future and a past she is mending, and that he has only cables; Dev says that is the silliest thing he has ever heard.

beats.scene: A girl sits on a stool with a violin and shaking hands
beats.summary: At Tilly's last lesson before the recital, the girl's hands shake, and she whispers that she is afraid she will freeze on stage.

beats.scene: A woman kneels beside a girl and speaks gently to her
beats.summary: Odile does not lie; she tells Tilly that her own arm once shook, and that the first thing is to breathe and think of one friend in the room.

beats.scene: A man records a girl playing while she watches him through headphones
beats.summary: Sam, who has been listening at the door, offers to record Tilly and plays it back, so she can hear for herself how well she plays.

beats.scene: Two people sit at a laptop at midnight with headphones and tea
beats.summary: On the last night of the album they finish the mix together, and Sam asks if Odile's violin may open the very first track.

beats.scene: A man's finger hovers over a send button on a laptop screen
beats.summary: On Friday morning Sam cannot press send, until Odile puts her hand over his, and together they click and send the album to Ms Pereira.

beats.scene: A woman and a man wait beside a silent phone on a table
beats.summary: Ms Pereira replies in an hour with only a few words: Thank you, we will tell you soon; and Sam spends the whole afternoon pretending he is not waiting.

beats.scene: A woman practises a violin piece by a window as a tall man listens
beats.summary: That evening Odile practises Tilly's piece again and again, and Sam promises he will be at the Corn Hall tomorrow with a microphone to record it.

beats.scene: A woman lies awake in a dark bedroom while the moon shines in
beats.summary: That night neither of them sleeps well; Odile stares at the ceiling, and through the wall she hears Sam turn over, and then, very softly, a single tap.

beats.scene: A girl in a blue dress waits outside a stone hall with her parents
beats.summary: On Saturday morning Tilly waits outside the Corn Hall in a blue dress, between her parents, with hands as cold as ice.

beats.scene: A woman ties a ribbon in a girl's hair in a small side room
beats.summary: Backstage Odile ties a ribbon in Tilly's hair and says she will be in the front row, so that Tilly can look only at her.

beats.scene: A hall full of parents, and a microphone at the back
beats.summary: The hall fills with parents and children; Sam sets up a microphone at the back, and Dev, Mrs Okonkwo and Mr Tavish take seats near him.

beats.scene: A boy plays a drum on a stage while a crowd laughs and claps
beats.summary: The first performers play: a boy with a drum, two sisters with recorders and a very serious girl on a cello, and each is applauded warmly.

beats.scene: A small girl in blue walks onto a lit stage
beats.summary: At last the announcer says Tilly Marsh, and she walks to the middle of the stage, very small in the bright light, and lifts her violin.

beats.scene: A girl stops playing on a stage with her bow hanging in the air
beats.summary: She begins well, plays eight bars, and then her mind goes blank; her bow stops in the air, and Tilly freezes.

beats.scene: A woman half rises from her seat in the front row of a hall
beats.summary: In the front row Odile remembers the dark hall, the pencil and the trembling bow, and she knows exactly how cold the silence feels.

beats.scene: A woman climbs the steps of a stage with a violin in her hand
beats.summary: Odile takes her violin from its case, walks up the stage steps in front of two hundred people and stands at Tilly's side.

beats.scene: A woman and a girl play violins side by side on a stage
beats.summary: She whispers breathe and plays the first soft bars, and Tilly's bow comes down and finds the tune as they play together.

beats.scene: A girl plays alone on a stage while a woman lowers her violin
beats.summary: Little by little Odile fades out and lets Tilly play alone, and the girl finishes the piece to the last note without a single shake.

beats.scene: A hall of people stands and cheers while a girl bows on a stage
beats.summary: The hall explodes in applause, the people stand, and Tilly bows deeply and then runs to hug her teacher.

beats.scene: A man at the back of a hall wipes his eyes beside a microphone
beats.summary: At the back Sam wipes his eyes with his sleeve and presses stop on the recording, while Mr Tavish blows his nose loudly and says it was not bad for a staircase.

beats.scene: A woman looks at her own steady right hand in a quiet side room
beats.summary: In the side room Odile looks at her right hand, which is perfectly still, and realises that she has just played in front of two hundred people.

beats.scene: Two people walk down a street at evening as lamps come on
beats.summary: In the evening, as the lamps come on, Odile and Sam walk home together along Lamplighter Lane, carrying the stand and the microphone.

beats.scene: Two people stand under a streetlamp, one looking at the ground
beats.summary: Under the lamp outside number 22, Odile admits she dreads moving out, because nothing else in her life has ever sounded like this.

beats.scene: A man looks up at a woman under a streetlamp
beats.summary: Sam says he is bad at saying things, but he does not want to move either; not to Kiln Street, not anywhere without her.

beats.scene: A man holds up a letter from a landlord outside a tall building
beats.summary: He pulls out a letter and explains that last week he wrote to Mr Quill, who is back from abroad: Mrs Okonkwo's Flat 3B is free to let at the end of the month.

beats.scene: A woman laughs under a lamp while a man waits nervously
beats.summary: Odile laughs with surprise and asks if he is asking her to move in as a flatmate, or as something more.

beats.scene: Two people kiss on a landing under a round window
beats.summary: Sam says, more, much more, and Odile says yes; they climb the stairs and kiss on the top landing, under the round window.

beats.scene: An old woman peeks through a door on a landing while a cat watches
beats.summary: A door opens a crack on the third floor, and Mrs Okonkwo's voice says, quite calmly, that it was about time; then Biscuit's tail swishes.

beats.scene: Two people sit at a kitchen table with a plan of an empty flat
beats.summary: That night they sit at the kitchen table and draw a plan of Flat 3B: two bedrooms, a big front room and a piano, and no coin toss is needed.

beats.scene: A tall tanned man in tweed stands at a door with a suitcase
beats.summary: On Sunday morning there is a knock, and Mr Quill, the landlord, tall, tanned and in a tweed coat, stands there with a suitcase and apologises for the mix-up.

beats.scene: A landlord looks up at a high ceiling in a sunny front room
beats.summary: Mrs Okonkwo lets them all into Flat 3B, and Mr Quill admires the high ceilings and says the echo in this building is the best in the city.

beats.scene: A landlord holds a lease with two lines for names and looks serious
beats.summary: Mr Quill asks them seriously whether they are sure, because a lease with two names on one page is a promise; they look at each other and say yes.

beats.scene: A woman phones while a man crosses two flats off a list
beats.summary: Odile rings Ms Vane to cancel the two flats on Harbour Road and Kiln Street, and Ms Vane says she is delighted, and that her computer is, too.

beats.scene: A cheerful man shouts into a phone held far from a tall man's ear
beats.summary: Sam rings Dev with the news, and Dev shouts so loudly that Sam has to hold the phone away; he says he knew it, he always knew it.

beats.scene: A small elegant woman talks on a phone in a country kitchen
beats.summary: Odile phones her mother, who cries out two keys, I knew it, and promises to come soon with plum jam.

beats.scene: A woman in a blazer smiles as she speaks into a phone
beats.summary: Then Ms Pereira rings with the news that Sam has been waiting for: the choir adores the album, and a record company wants to release it in the autumn.

beats.scene: A man sits on a floor against a wall beside a woman
beats.summary: Sam hangs up, slides down the wall onto the floor and says in a whisper that his studio is safe; Odile sits beside him and takes his hand.

beats.scene: An old woman pats a dusty piano in a sunlit front room
beats.summary: Mrs Okonkwo tells them the piano will not go to the sea, because it hates salt air, and so it belongs to Flat 3B and to them.

beats.scene: Two people carry boxes down a staircase while a grey cat watches
beats.summary: On moving day Sam and Odile carry their boxes down one flight of stairs, with Dev and Mr Tavish helping, while Biscuit supervises from a step.

beats.scene: A woman touches a pale line on a wooden floor in an empty flat
beats.summary: Odile takes a last look at the empty flat and touches the pale line on the hall floor where the tape once lay, and Sam's hand finds hers.

beats.scene: A taxi waits at a kerb as an old woman hugs a young woman
beats.summary: A taxi waits at the kerb for Mrs Okonkwo, who hugs Odile and Sam and tells them to mind the echo; Biscuit leaps from his basket and runs back inside.

beats.scene: A tall landlord hands a ring with two keys to two smiling people
beats.summary: Mr Quill appears at the door of Flat 3B and hands them two keys on one ring, and says that this time the agent had not made a mistake.

beats.scene: Two keys are held in two hands in front of an open front door
beats.summary: They each take a key, and at the same moment push them into the same lock, and both keys turn with a soft, satisfied click.

beats.scene: Two people stand in an empty sunlit room with a dusty piano
beats.summary: Inside the big front room, with sunlight on the floor and the piano by the wall, they stand for a long moment, and no tape is needed.

beats.scene: A woman sticks a note on a fridge with a lemon magnet
beats.summary: That evening the lemon magnet goes up on the new fridge, and Odile writes the first note of their new home: Soup?; Sam adds a tiny moustache to it.

beats.scene: A woman teaches a row of children violin in a bright room
beats.summary: In the autumn Odile teaches the choir children and plays in a little quartet at weddings, as Grandpa Luc once did, and Sam's studio is never empty.

beats.scene: A choir of children sings on a stage in a stone hall at night
beats.summary: On the night of the album launch at the Corn Hall, the choir sings from the stage, Arlo in tune at last, and Mr Tavish sits in the front row in his best tie.

beats.scene: A man and a woman each hold a key before a glowing doorway
beats.summary: That evening they climb the steps of Lamplighter Lane, each with a key in hand, and open the door of their home together with their two keys.

A1A2: Odile climbed four floors with a suitcase and a violin.
On the third floor, a grey cat watched her from a door.
At the top, she stopped and took a long, slow breath.
She opened the door, and a man in headphones was inside.
The man jumped and said, “You have the wrong flat.”
They put their rental papers on the counter, side by side.
Each of them tried a key, and both keys opened the door.
They called the letting agency, and Ms Vane answered quickly.
Ms Vane said that nothing else was free for a month.
Neither of them had a home to go back to.
Odile phoned a friend, but her friend was away.
The hotels were too expensive, even for one night.
Sam said, “We could share it, just for a month.”
Odile looked at his many boxes, wires, and microphones.
She picked up her suitcase, but she had nowhere to go.
Ms Vane called back and offered them half the rent.
They walked through the flat and looked at every room.
They both wanted the bedroom, and neither would give way.
Sam found a coin, and Odile called heads.
Heads won, so Odile took the bedroom and Sam took the study.
Alone in her room, Odile opened the violin case slowly.
In the kitchen, they found one kettle and two mugs.
Sam went out and came back with a roll of blue tape.
Sam pressed a blue line down the middle of the hall.
The bathroom was on Odile's side, which was a problem.
They divided the fridge shelves and the kitchen cupboards fairly.
They ate dinner at opposite ends of the kitchen table.
At seven, Odile took out her violin and began scales.
In the study, Sam heard scales through the thin wall.
He knocked on the wall, and she shouted back at him.
At nine, she stopped playing, and the flat grew quiet.
In the dark, she heard Sam laughing through the thin wall.
At midnight, she was still awake, listening to him hum.
In the morning, a sock hung on the bathroom door handle.
In the kitchen, they both reached for the only kettle.
They agreed to write rules: violin at four, recordings at nine.
They stuck the timetable on the fridge with a magnet.
Soon, little notes began to appear on the fridge door.
At first the notes were angry, but slowly they became funny.
Odile drew a tiny violin, and Sam drew a funny microphone.
On the fourth afternoon, a grey cat jumped through the window.
Sam tried to catch the cat, but it ran away.
Odile and Sam both got down on the floor.
The cat walked out and sat on the violin case.
A knock came: it was Mrs Okonkwo from Flat 3B.
Mrs Okonkwo smiled and said, “You two make a lovely noise together.”
Mrs Okonkwo noticed the tape and raised her eyebrows.
On Thursday, they went down to Mrs Okonkwo's flat for tea.
Mrs Okonkwo told them her daughter wanted her to move.
Mrs Okonkwo asked Odile to play, and Odile played softly.
That night, Odile put a letter in the bottom drawer.
The next morning, Sam's phone rang, and he jumped.
He told Odile at the fridge, and she smiled and congratulated him.
Sam drew a plan: eight songs, forty children, and four weeks.
First, Sam tested the study, but the sounds were wrong.
He carried his microphone through the flat to every room.
Sam sat among his cables, tired and worried about the work.
At four, Odile began to play, but she stopped suddenly.
Sam heard the silence and sent Dev a message about soup.
He burned the first pot, but the second was good.
A pot of soup sat on the tape, with a small note.
Odile found the pot and read the note on the lid.
She tasted the soup, and it was really very good.
She wrote a short note and asked him to come and hear Bach.
Sam read the note and was unsure what it meant.
At six, Odile played Bach in the hall, and Sam listened.
When she finished, Sam said only, “Thank you.”
Nine-year-old Tilly came for a lesson, because she had a concert soon.
Sam hid in the study, but he heard one peg slip.
The chalk worked, and Tilly smiled for the first time.
Sam carried the recycling down and dropped a spoon.
He clapped his hands once and heard a long echo.
He ran upstairs and told Odile about the amazing echo.
On the landing, Odile played one long note, and it grew.
Mrs Okonkwo called up from below about the old choir.
A man in a dressing gown came out of Flat 2A.
At midnight, Sam hung his microphone from the stairs on a string.
Odile came out in her coat, and he pressed record.
Sam played it back through the headphones and stared.
Sam said softly, “You are not only a teacher.”
The next night, they sat on the stairs with mugs of tea.
Odile said, quietly, “I played in the City Orchestra for six years.”
Every year, each player had to audition for the conductor.
Then her arm shook, and she could not play any more.
She had told no one, not even her mother.
Sam said, “A chair is not a violin.”
Then Sam told her his own secret fear.
They shared a packet of biscuits, and Biscuit appeared.
In the morning, they felt shy, but the notes were kinder.
Odile's mother phoned, and she wanted to visit this weekend.
Sam said, “I am not offering a fix, only tea.”
They cleaned the whole flat from top to bottom.
On Friday evening, Mrs Brandt arrived carrying a heavy basket.
Odile said Sam was only a friend, and her mother looked surprised.
Sam cooked dinner for three people, and Mrs Brandt ate well.
In the kitchen, her mother whispered, “He is lovely.”
Mrs Brandt took the bedroom, and the others slept elsewhere.
On Saturday, her mother asked which night the orchestra played.
Odile told her mother the whole truth, from beginning to end.
Her mother stood up and hugged her, and said she was proud.
On Sunday, Mrs Brandt left, and she kissed them both.
On Monday, Odile offered to help Sam with the choir.
Ms Pereira visited the stairs and clapped her hands once.
On Saturday, forty children filled the stairs, whispering and giggling.
Odile showed the children how to stand tall and breathe.
The smallest boy, Arlo, sang very loudly and out of tune.
The first takes went wrong: a cough, a loud noise, a lorry.
Mr Tavish came back early and stopped in the doorway.
Mr Tavish sat on the stair and listened to the end.
They recorded the quiet song, and the third time was perfect.
On Sunday, Dev came with a huge pot and some shopping.
Dev took over the kitchen and gave Sam many orders.
At dinner, Dev told stories about Sam, and everyone laughed.
After dinner, Odile played a short piece for them both.
At the sink, Dev told Odile that Sam was very kind.
At the door, Dev whispered to Sam, “Say it before the month ends.”
On Monday, Ms Vane rang with news: two flats were ready.
Both said, “That is great news,” but neither meant it.
They avoided each other all day, in their own rooms.
That night, Odile tapped twice on the wall, and Sam answered.
On Wednesday, Dev sent Odile a message about Sam's birthday.
Odile decided to bake a cake, though she had never baked.
On his birthday, she baked while Sam was away at a meeting.
The cake came out crooked, and it tasted terrible.
Mrs Okonkwo came up and said that a cake need not be good.
Sam came home early and stopped in the kitchen doorway.
Odile lit three candles and said, “It is probably awful.”
Sam took a big bite and said, “It is perfect.”
Then she played “Happy Birthday” on her violin, slowly.
Sam gave her a small envelope with a tiny drive inside.
That evening, they danced in the kitchen to music.
Sam said they should take it up, and they pulled up the tape.
Odile put the ball of tape on a shelf beside the magnet.
That night, a great storm arrived and rain beat on the roof.
In the night, Odile heard a drip and went to the study.
Odile threw her coat over the hard drive and shouted.
Sam ran in and carried the hard drive to a dry shelf.
They put out every bowl and pan, and they phoned for help.
Mr Tavish appeared with a ladder and a sheet of plastic.
Afterwards, they sat on the bed holding the hard drive.
Their hug lasted a little too long, and neither moved.
At dawn, Sam made three copies of the whole album.
In the morning, Ms Vane arrived with two keys in two envelopes.
They each took a key without saying a word.
They packed their boxes in silence, not looking at each other.
Odile took down the notes from the fridge, one by one.
By evening, the flat was empty, and every step echoed.
Mrs Okonkwo invited Odile down and told her some news.
She added that Odile and Sam were two foolish people.
Odile climbed upstairs and heard Sam talking in the study.
Dev met Sam at a café and gave him a stern look.
Sam said, “She has her violin, and I only have cables.”
At her last lesson, Tilly's hands shook as she played.
Odile told Tilly the truth: “My arm shook, too.”
Sam recorded Tilly and played it back through headphones.
On the last night, they finished the mix of the album.
On Friday, Sam could not make himself press the button.
Ms Pereira answered with only a few words: “We will tell you soon.”
That evening, Odile practised again, and Sam listened.
That night, neither of them slept well in the dark.
On Saturday, Tilly waited outside the Corn Hall in a blue dress.
Backstage, Odile tied a ribbon in Tilly's hair.
The hall filled with parents, and Sam set up a microphone at the back.
The first children played, and the hall clapped warmly for each.
At last they called Tilly's name, and she walked onto the stage.
She played eight bars, and then her mind went blank.
In the front row, Odile remembered her own silence on stage.
Odile took her violin and walked up the stage steps.
Odile whispered “Breathe,” and they began to play together.
Odile stopped playing, and Tilly finished the piece alone.
The hall exploded with applause, and everyone stood to cheer.
At the back, Sam wiped his eyes and stopped the recording.
Odile looked at her right hand, and it was perfectly still.
In the evening, Odile and Sam walked home along the lane.
Under a lamp, Odile said, “I dread the move.”
Sam said, “I am bad at saying things, but I do not want to go.”
He took a letter from his pocket and held it up.
Odile laughed and asked if he meant a friend, or something more.
Sam said he meant more, and Odile said yes, and they kissed.
A door opened a crack, and Mrs Okonkwo said, “At last.”
That night, they drew a plan of Flat 3B at the table.
On Sunday morning, a knock came: it was Mr Quill, the landlord.
Mrs Okonkwo showed them Flat 3B, and Mr Quill admired it.
Mr Quill asked them both if they were sure, and they looked at each other.
Odile phoned Ms Vane to cancel the two other flats.
Sam called Dev, and Dev shouted so loudly that Sam held the phone away.
Odile phoned her mother, who shouted that she knew it all along.
Then Ms Pereira rang with the news Sam had waited for.
Sam sat on the floor and whispered, “My studio is safe.”
Mrs Okonkwo said the piano would stay in Flat 3B.
On moving day, they carried boxes down one floor of stairs.
Odile took a last look at the empty flat above.
A taxi came for Mrs Okonkwo, and she hugged them both.
Mr Quill gave them two keys on one ring.
They tried both keys in the same lock, and both turned.
Inside, they stood in the big bright front room for a moment.
That evening, Odile put a note on the new fridge: “Soup?”
In the autumn, Odile taught the choir children and played at weddings.
On the night of the launch, the choir sang at the Corn Hall.
That evening, they opened their door together with two keys.
B1B2: Odile Brandt dragged her suitcase and her violin up four floors of narrow stairs. In her pocket was the key to Flat 4B, her new home for the year.
On the third floor, a grey cat sat in a half-open doorway and watched her pass. A kind old voice from inside called out that the top flat had a lovely echo.
At the top of the stairs, Odile stopped and took a long breath. She wanted a quiet place to start again, although she had told nobody why.
Odile opened the door and stopped still on the doormat. A man with large headphones around his neck stood among the boxes, and he was holding a key exactly like hers.
The man jumped and dropped a long cable on the floor. He pulled off his headphones and said, quite politely, that she must have the wrong flat.
The man said his name was Sam Ferreira, and that this was his flat. They put their papers side by side on the counter and saw that both were for Flat 4B, and both began today.
Odile wanted proof, so they went back to the door together. Sam's key turned the lock, and then hers did too, and neither of them said anything for a moment.
They rang the agency and put Ms Vane on speaker. She said the flat had been booked twice by a computer mistake, and she was very, very sorry.
Ms Vane checked her list and said that every flat and hotel in the city was full. A big festival had come to town, and nothing else would be free for a month.
Odile's old flat had been sold to a new owner last week. Sam's lease had ended on Friday, and both of them had already paid a deposit here.
Odile phoned an old friend from music school, but she was away on tour. Sam rang his friend Dev, whose small flat was already full of his cousins.
Odile looked up hotels on her phone, one after another, and none of them was cheap. The cheapest room was so expensive that one night would cost her a week of lessons.
Sam cleared his throat and suggested that they could simply share the flat. Odile stared at him as if he had proposed sharing a toothbrush.
She pointed at the wires, the boxes and the microphones spread across the floor. She had never lived with anyone who owned so many cables, she said, and she did not plan to start.
Odile picked up her suitcase and walked to the door. She looked down the four flights of stairs and knew she had nowhere to take it.
Just then Ms Vane called back with an offer. If they both stayed for the month, each of them would pay only half the rent.
They walked slowly through the flat and looked carefully at every room. There was a long hall, a noisy kitchen, one bedroom, and a tiny study with a sofa that was far too short.
Both of them wanted the bedroom, and they said so at the same time. Odile needed it for her violin, and Sam knew the sofa would never fit him.
Sam found a coin in his pocket and tossed it high in the air. Odile called heads, and they both watched it spin until it hit the floor.
The coin landed heads up, and Odile took the bedroom. Sam folded himself onto the short sofa, set up his favourite microphone, Winnie, and called through the wall that it was only for a month.
Alone in the bedroom, Odile opened her violin case and touched the strings. She promised herself that she would practise every single afternoon, however hard it felt.
In the kitchen they found one kettle, two mugs and half a loaf of bread. It was not clear whose shelf was whose, and they both said so loudly.
Sam went out to the corner shop and came back twenty minutes later. He was holding a roll of blue masking tape and looking very proud of himself.
On his knees, Sam pressed a straight line of tape down the middle of the hall. It ran on across the front room and stopped at the kitchen wall.
Odile pointed out that the bathroom was on her side of the line. They agreed that Sam could cross it if a sock was not hanging on the door handle.
They divided the kitchen with strips of tape and a marker pen. Odile took the top shelf, Sam took the bottom, and each of them was given one pan.
That evening Odile cooked plain pasta and Sam made beans on toast. They ate at opposite ends of the table without saying very much.
The whole afternoon had gone on the stairs and the phone calls, so Odile had not practised yet. At seven she tuned her violin and began with slow, loud scales.
In the study, Sam was recording a quiet voice for a podcast. The scales leaked through the thin wall into his microphone, and the take was ruined.
Sam knocked on the wall, and then he called out in a louder voice, because the music did not stop. Odile shouted back that she had to practise, and that the wall was certainly not her fault.
At nine o'clock Odile put her violin away, and the flat went quiet. Only the old pipes in the wall went on tapping softly, like a patient drummer.
Lying in the dark, Odile heard a low laugh through the wall. Sam was listening to his own recordings, and every few minutes he laughed again.
At midnight she was still awake, staring at the dark ceiling. Through the wall she heard a goose honk on a recording, and Sam humming along as if the goose were a singer.
