He held it up like a trophy and announced that if the flat was going to be shared, it had better be shared fairly and visibly. Odile looked at the tape and wondered whether she had just agreed to live with an engineer.

Sam knelt in the hall and pressed the blue tape to the floorboards in one long, ruler-straight line, smoothing every inch with his thumb. The line ran the whole length of the hall, turned sharply across the front room and ended at the kitchen wall, so that the flat was cut neatly into two halves. Odile watched from the bedroom doorway, impressed and appalled in about equal measure, like a customer watching a magician.

Odile pointed out, with some satisfaction, that the only bathroom in the flat lay entirely on her side of the line. After a short and dignified argument they agreed that Sam might cross the tape to use it, provided that a sock hanging from the door handle was always taken to mean that the room was occupied. It was quite the strangest treaty that either of them had ever been asked to sign.

With a roll of tape and a marker pen they carved up the kitchen as carefully as two nations drawing a border. Odile took the top fridge shelf and the left cupboards, Sam took the bottom shelf and the right ones, and each of them was granted exactly one frying pan and one saucepan. The toaster, which neither could bear to give up, was declared neutral territory, to be shared in peace and defended by nobody.

That evening Odile boiled a modest pan of plain pasta, while Sam, with equal dignity, assembled beans on toast, and the two of them carried their plates to opposite ends of the kitchen table. They chewed in a silence broken only by the clink of forks and the occasional shudder of the pipes behind the wall. It was the kind of quiet in which two people notice every sound the other makes.

The double booking had swallowed the whole afternoon, and so Odile had not yet played a note that day, which made her restless and cross with herself. At seven o'clock she tuned her violin by the bedroom window and began with the long, slow scales she had practised since she was six years old. The notes were rich and clear, and they went straight through the wall like water through paper.

On the other side of the wall, Sam was recording a quiet voice for a podcast, and he had nearly finished a perfect take. Odile's scales crept through the thin plaster, climbed into Winnie's delicate ribbon and arrived on his screen as a shimmering ghost line that no editing could remove. He sat back, stared at the wall and glared at it as though the wall itself were to blame.

Sam knocked on the wall with a polite knuckle, called out a polite request, and then, receiving no answer, called out a good deal less politely. Odile broke off mid-phrase and shouted back through the plaster that she had to practise, that the wall was not her fault and that he had agreed to share the flat of his own free will. For a moment the only sound was both of them breathing angrily on either side of a single wall.

At nine o'clock, a little ashamed of her shouting, Odile lowered her bow and laid the violin in its case. The flat sank into a hush that was not quite silence, because somewhere inside the walls the old pipes went on tapping and sighing like a patient drummer rehearsing for a concert nobody had booked. She turned off the lamp and lay down on a bed that did not yet feel like hers.

Lying in the dark with her eyes open, Odile heard a low, warm laugh drift through the wall, and then another, and then a third. Sam was working late on something that amused him enormously, and each time he laughed, the sound broke into her tired thoughts like a small bell in a quiet church. She was annoyed at first, and then, to her own considerable surprise, a little curious as well.

By midnight Odile had counted every crack in the ceiling and was still wide awake. Through the wall came the loud honk of a goose from one of Sam's recordings, followed at once by Sam himself humming along in a soft, serious voice, as if the goose were a soloist who needed accompanying. It was ridiculous, and it was the first thing all day that had made her want to smile.

In the morning, Odile shuffled down the hall, yawning, and found a grey sock draped on the bathroom handle like a tiny flag of occupation. She leaned against the wall and listened to the water running, and running, and running, while her own turn crept further and further away. Sam, it seemed, took his showers the way other people took their holidays, slowly and with great enjoyment.

In the kitchen they reached for the only kettle at exactly the same moment, and their hands stopped an inch apart over the handle. Neither wished to be the first to retreat, so they stood there in the thin morning light with their empty mugs, glaring politely, while the pipes cleared their throats behind the wall. It was, in its own peculiar way, the most formal breakfast either of them had ever experienced.

Over lukewarm tea, they agreed that the only way to survive was to put everything in writing. Odile would play her violin between four and six every afternoon, and Sam would record only after nine at night, which left the hours between as a kind of demilitarised zone for dinner and sighing. They shook hands on the bargain, rather stiffly, like two diplomats at the end of a long war.

The finished timetable was fixed to the fridge door with a magnet shaped like a lemon, and for a moment they both stood back and admired it. Then Sam picked up a pen and added a small line at the bottom, requesting no scales before breakfast, to which Odile added, in neat capitals, that no goose should be played after midnight either. In a single afternoon the humble fridge had become the first parliament of the flat.

Within a day, the fridge door had begun to fill with notes, written in two very different hands, one slanting and hurried, the other upright and precise. Sam asked her, in capitals, to stop moving his pan to the other shelf, and Odile replied underneath that a pan was not a pet and did not need to be guarded. Neither of them could yet tell whether they were quarrelling or simply playing a new kind of game.

For a day or two the notes grew sharper, with an accusation about damp socks on the radiator, a complaint about a pan left unwashed overnight and a pointed reminder to read the timetable. Then, almost without either of them noticing, the tone began to soften into teasing, and a small joke would slip into the corner of a complaint like a coin into a pocket. Slowly the fridge had stopped being a courtroom and begun, quite without permission, to be a stage.

One morning, in the corner of a stern note about the bins, Odile drew a very small violin with a very large frown. By the time she returned from her lesson that evening, Sam had added a microphone wearing a splendid curled moustache and apologising in a speech bubble for the pan. She read it three times, standing alone at the fridge, and was careful to wipe the smile from her face before anyone could see.

On the fourth afternoon, while Odile was in the middle of a difficult passage, a grey shape sprang from the fire escape, sailed through the open study window and landed in the middle of Sam's desk. A cup rattled, a lamp rocked and three cables slid slowly to the floor, while the cat sat down in the wreckage and began calmly to wash a paw. Odile lowered her bow, and the whole afternoon's practice came to a sudden and astonished halt.

Sam lunged for the cat with both hands, but it slipped through his fingers like a handful of smoke and shot off down the long hall. A stack of boxes toppled over behind it with a crash, and out of one of them rolled a tangle of tape, a single shoe and a very surprised stapler. Odile, abandoning her violin on the bed, ran out into the hall to join the hunt with a sudden and unexpected thrill.

The cat vanished beneath the sofa, and two grown adults got down on their hands and knees to look for it, one from each side. In their excitement they crawled across the blue tape line without noticing it at all, and met nose to nose in the dusty dark, each holding a torch and an expression of deep embarrassment. It was Odile who started laughing first, and once she had begun, she could not possibly stop.

The cat strolled out from under the sofa as if nothing had happened, crossed the room and settled itself on top of Odile's violin case with the satisfied air of a landlord. Odile and Sam froze where they knelt, afraid that the slightest movement would send it running again, and the whole flat held its breath. The only sound in the room was the deep, rumbling engine of the cat's contented purr.

A brisk knock sounded at the front door, and when Sam opened it, a tiny old woman in a green cardigan was standing on the mat with her arms already held out. She introduced herself as Mrs Okonkwo of Flat 3B, apologised graciously for her cat, whose name was Biscuit. She explained that he had been climbing out of her window to visit the top flat ever since the last tenant left.

Mrs Okonkwo scooped up Biscuit in one practised movement and looked down at the pair of them, still sitting on the floor with their torches and their dusty knees. A slow, wise smile spread across her face, and she remarked that she had heard them through the floor all week and that together they made a lovely noise. Neither of them knew quite where to look, and both of them suddenly found the floor fascinating.

On her way out, Mrs Okonkwo noticed the blue tape running down the middle of the hall, and one eyebrow rose slowly above the rim of her glasses. She said nothing about it, which was more eloquent than a speech, and instead invited them both down to Flat 3B for tea on Thursday at four, adding that she would not take no for an answer. Biscuit, perched in her arms, looked back over her shoulder at them with an expression of open triumph.

On Thursday afternoon they went down one flight of stairs and found Flat 3B larger and grander than their own, with ceilings so high that the sound of the teaspoons seemed to float up and stay there. A dusty piano stood against one wall, and on the shelf above it a row of photographs showed a smiling woman on a windy beach. Mrs Okonkwo explained that this was her daughter Ngozi, who lived by the sea.

Over a second cup of strong tea, Mrs Okonkwo confided that her daughter Ngozi had been begging her for a year to come and live by the sea. She was thinking about it slowly, she said, the way one thinks about cold water, because she had lived in this building for forty years and every stair of it knew her name. Odile saw how tightly the old woman held her cup, and understood that the decision was not yet made.

When Mrs Okonkwo asked, with great simplicity, whether Odile would play something for an old woman, Odile's first instinct was to refuse. But she looked at the piano, the high ceiling and the patient old face, and after a long moment she lifted her violin and played a slow, sweet air that filled the room to the corners. Sam, standing in the doorway with his cup forgotten in his hand, did not move once from beginning to end.

That night, when the flat was dark, Odile took a letter from the bottom of her suitcase, the one with the City Orchestra's crest at the top. It said, in cold and courteous words, that she had not kept her chair after the yearly audition, and she had read it so often that the folds were soft as cloth. She tucked it into the bottom drawer, beneath her winter socks, where nobody at home would ever find it.

The next morning Sam's phone rang, and he answered it with a mouth full of toast and a face that slowly went from sleepy to dazzled. It was Ms Pereira, the director of the Larkspur Children's Choir, calling to say that the choir had chosen him over three bigger studios to record their first album. He hung up, found a thick pen and circled a date four weeks away on the calendar with a hand that was not quite steady.

Sam blurted out the news to Odile at the fridge, still holding the pen, and she congratulated him at once, warmly and without a trace of teasing. He thanked her and tried to smile, but she noticed that his face had turned slightly pale, as if the good news had arrived with a bill attached. It was a look that she knew very well from her own mirror, and she did not like to see it.

Sam spread a large sheet of paper on the counter and explained the plan with the speed of a man who had been thinking about it for months. There would be eight songs, forty children, three weekends of recording, and a final week of mixing, and the whole thing depended on finding one quiet, perfect room with a sound that made small voices shine. He tapped the paper with his pen, looked up at the ceiling and let out a long, unhappy sigh.

He began, of course, with the study, and listened through his headphones with his eyes closed and his head tilted like a bird's. The street sent up its steady growl of buses and taxis, the fridge in the kitchen hummed a flat and unfortunate note, and every few minutes the pipes in the wall let out a knock like a mischievous guest. In short, the little room was a thief of silence, and it stole a good deal more than it gave.

Carrying Winnie before him like a lantern, Sam went from room to room and listened to each of them as a doctor listens to a chest. The kitchen was full of clatter and hum, the long hall swallowed every sound into a dull flatness, and the bathroom echoed so wildly that his own whisper came back to him like a ghost in a tiled cave. He sat down on the cold edge of the bath, lowered Winnie carefully to his knees and groaned.

Back in the study, he sat down on the floor among the coils of cable, feeling like a sailor adrift on a sea of black rope. He had won the most important job of his life, and he could not find a single quiet room to do it in. His small studio, which he had built with a loan and a great deal of hope, depended entirely on the answer, and in despair he tossed his headphones onto the sofa.

At four o'clock, according to the timetable, Odile began her practice, but the old tightness crept into her right arm and her bow began to tremble against the strings. She broke off in the middle of a phrase, rested the violin on her knee and sat very still, and a heavy silence spread through the flat like water. In the study, Sam lifted his head and listened to the gap where the music should have been.

Sam did not know what to say to the silence from the other room, and so he did what he did best, which was to find a different way to answer it. He texted his friend Dev, a cheerful cook, to ask for the simplest soup in the world, and Dev replied within a minute with seven messages, three photographs and a firm warning about salt. Sam read them all twice over, standing in the middle of the kitchen like a man studying a map.

The first pot of lentil soup burned to a black crust and filled the kitchen with a smell that sent the neighbours' windows flying open. Sam scraped, scrubbed, opened every window and began again, and this time, with Dev's seven messages pinned to the fridge, the soup came out thick, golden and fragrant with cumin. He lifted the pot in both hands and carried it down the hall toward the blue tape.

Sam set the steaming pot down on the very centre of the blue tape and propped a note against its lid, written in his slanting, hurried hand. It said, quite simply, that soup was allowed to cross the tape, and that nobody would be asked any questions. Then he retreated to the study and shut the door with exaggerated quiet, like a man leaving an offering at a shrine.

When Odile finally opened her bedroom door, she found the pot of soup waiting on the tape, its steam curling slowly toward the ceiling. She read the note on the lid twice, and a stubborn part of her wanted to push the pot back across the line untouched, because she did not like to owe anyone a favour. But the smell of cumin and warm lentils had already crept into her stomach, and her stomach had no pride at all.

She dipped a spoon into the golden soup and tasted it with an expression of stern suspicion, which melted away almost at once. It was thick, warm and deeply savoury, with a hint of lemon at the end, and before she realised what she was doing she had eaten two whole bowls standing at the counter. She had not eaten a proper, hot meal since the long and tiring morning of the stairs.

Odile washed her bowl, dried it carefully and stood for a long moment with a pen in her hand, wondering how a person said thank you to a man she was still half inclined to dislike. In the end she wrote, in her neat upright capitals, that the soup was approved and that he was welcome to come and listen to some Bach at six if he cared to. She stuck the note to the lid of the empty pot and set it back on the line.

Sam read the note three times and could not decide whether it was an invitation, a threat or a joke, since Odile's handwriting gave nothing away. He worked through the afternoon with one eye on the clock, and at two minutes to six, with the air of a man stepping into cold water, he slowly took off his headphones. The study fell quiet, and he realised how loudly his own heart was beating.

At six o'clock exactly Odile stood in the long hall, with the evening light pouring through the front windows, and began a slow movement by Bach. Sam sat down on the floor on his own side of the tape, leaned his head back against the wall and closed his eyes. For the first time since he had arrived, the flat felt like a place made for sound, and neither of them spoke or wished to.

When the last note had faded into the corners of the hall, Sam rose slowly from the floor and looked at her as though he wanted to say a great deal. What he said, in the end, was a single quiet thank you, and then he returned to the study and closed the door behind him, leaving Odile to wonder what the silence meant. It meant, though she could not know it, that he was busy rewriting everything he thought he knew about her.

The next afternoon Odile's pupil Tilly Marsh arrived for her weekly lesson, brought up the four flights by her father, who left her at the door with a quick pat on the head. She was nine years old and very shy, with a plait down her back and a violin case clutched to her chest like a shield, and she was to play at a recital in the Corn Hall in two weeks. She looked around the strange flat, and at the blue line on the floor, with enormous eyes.

Sam did his best to be invisible during the lesson, but his ears, which were trained to notice the smallest wobble in a note, kept catching the same tiny flaw. A tuning peg on Tilly's violin was slipping every few minutes, and finally he came out of the study with a stub of chalk in his hand and offered a gentle suggestion. A little chalk on the peg, he explained, would help it to grip, and he held out the stub like a peace offering.

The chalk worked at once, the peg held firm, and Tilly smiled for the first time that afternoon, a small, surprised smile that lit up her whole face. Then she turned to her teacher and asked, in the loud and perfectly clear voice that nine-year-olds reserve for embarrassing questions, whether the tall man was her husband. Odile went pink to the tips of her ears, and Sam disappeared into the study as fast as a mouse into a hole.

The next evening Sam carried the recycling down the stairs in a clinking paper bag, and halfway down a spoon slipped out and bounced on the stone steps. It rang, and went on ringing, bright and clear, and the sound travelled up and down the stairwell and came home again with a shimmer that stopped him dead. He stood perfectly still on the cold stone landing with his head cocked and his mouth a little open.

He clapped his hands once, sharply, and the stairwell answered with a long, golden echo that seemed to hang in the air like a held breath. Forgetting the recycling entirely, he ran up and down all four flights, clapping, humming and calling out single words to test each landing, while the bag of bottles sat forgotten on the bottom step. At the very top, under the round window, the echo was best of all, long and golden and full of light.

Sam burst into the flat, out of breath and glowing, and told Odile that the stairwell was the most beautiful recording room he had ever heard. Odile, who had been peacefully reading, put down her book and pointed out that a staircase was a strange place to make an album and that she was not at all convinced. He grabbed her sleeve and begged her to come and listen, and against her better judgment she went.

On the top landing, she lifted her violin with a sceptical frown and drew a single long note from the A string. The sound unfolded and bloomed around them, rising up the stairwell and falling back in soft waves, so that it seemed that three violins were playing instead of one. She stopped, lowered her bow slowly and looked at Sam with something that was very close to astonishment.

Below them, a door opened, and Mrs Okonkwo leaned out in her green cardigan with Biscuit draped over her arm like a scarf. She called up that the whole building had always loved that echo, and that years ago the old residents' choir had sung carols on those stairs every Christmas Eve until the neighbours cried. She told them, with a wink, to mind the echo, because it kept every secret and gave it back.

A door banged open on the floor below, and a grey-haired man in a tartan dressing gown stepped out and scowled up the stairwell with the full force of forty years as a postman. He introduced himself as Mr Tavish of Flat 2A and informed them that the stairs were for walking on and not for concerts, and that he took a nap every afternoon. Sam promised, very humbly, to be as quiet as a mouse in the daytime, and the man retreated, unconvinced.

Mr Tavish, according to Mrs Okonkwo, always spent the weekend at his sister's by the river, so at midnight the stairwell belonged to them. Sam hung Winnie from the banister on a length of string, ran a bundle of cables down the steps like a mountaineer's rope, and set up a little glowing tower of equipment on the landing. His hands moved with the quick certainty of someone who knew exactly what he was doing.

Odile appeared on the landing in a long coat thrown over her pyjamas, her hair tied up in a scarf, and her violin tucked under her chin as if she were going to a very strange concert. She played a few quiet notes, which the stairwell caught and carried upward like a flock of birds, and Sam pressed the red record button without taking his eyes off her. The little red light glowed in the darkness of the stairwell like the eye of some watchful creature.

Sam played back the recording through his headphones, and as he listened, his eyes grew wider and wider until he looked like a boy at a firework display. Without a word, he slipped the headphones off his own ears and held them out to Odile, and she put them on with a puzzled expression, expecting to hear a small thin scrap of sound. What she heard instead was so unlike anything she had expected that it made her catch her breath.

In the headphones, her own violin sounded warm, free and unhurried, quite unlike the tight and anxious tone she had been fighting for months. She listened to a sound that was hers and yet strange, as if someone she had forgotten had come back to speak. Sam told her quietly that she was not only a teacher, that she never had been, and for once she did not have a clever answer.

The next night, long after the street had gone quiet, Sam carried two steaming mugs of tea out to the landing and found Odile already sitting on the top step with her knees drawn up. He sat a few steps below her, and between them hung Winnie on her string, motionless and attentive, like a small and patient ghost. For a while neither of them said anything, and the stairwell kept their silence safe.

At last Odile began to speak, quietly, as though the stairwell were a confessional. She told him that for six years she had played second violin in the City Orchestra, that it had been the whole shape of her life, and that this spring she had lost her chair there. She said it in a flat, careful voice, like someone reading out a list of repairs.

Every year, she explained, every player had to audition again, alone on the empty stage, for the conductor, Mr Halloran, who sat in the dark hall with a pencil and a face that gave nothing away. She had known the piece for months and had played it perfectly a hundred times. She lifted her bow and drew a breath and began as steadily as she had ever done anything in her life.

Then, in the middle of the second page, her right arm began to tremble, as though a stranger had taken hold of it, and the sound broke into splinters. She could not play one clean bar until the end, and the dark hall seemed to swallow every note as it left her bow, while Mr Halloran's pencil scratched, quite gently, on his paper. She said that the scratching of that pencil was the loudest sound she had ever heard in her life.

She had told no one, she confessed, not her sister, not her friends, and certainly not her mother, who still told everyone in her village with shining pride that her daughter played in the City Orchestra. Every phone call, she said, felt like a small theft of that pride, and the lie had grown heavier with each week of silence. When she had finished, she stared down at her hands as if they belonged to someone else entirely.

Sam did not try to fix anything, and that was exactly what she needed. He thought for a moment, turned his mug slowly in his hands and said that a chair was only a piece of furniture. The violin she had played tonight, he added, had been quite as much hers as it had ever been, and although it was not a clever speech, it landed in the stairwell and rang there for a very long time.

Then, as if the stairwell had loosened something in him, Sam told her what he had told nobody, not even Dev. He had borrowed a great deal of money to build his small studio, and the choir album was the first real job that would pay it back. If it failed, the studio would fail too, and he had no other plan at all, and he laughed a short laugh that had no happiness in it.

Sam produced a rather squashed packet of biscuits from his pocket, and they shared it in the dark, passing the crumbs back and forth with great ceremony. Before long a soft pad of paws came up the stairs, and Biscuit appeared out of the shadows and installed himself between them with the air of a diplomat who has arrived exactly on time. Their laughter, small and tired, went curling up the stairwell and came back doubled.

In the morning, both of them woke with the shy, slightly dizzy feeling of people who have said too much in the dark and must now face it in daylight. They avoided each other's eyes over breakfast, but the notes on the fridge had changed in the night, and the tone of them was softer, a single word asking whether there was tea, and a single word saying yes. The line of blue tape still lay quietly between them on the floor, looking just a little foolish in the morning light.

That afternoon the phone rang, and Odile saw her mother's name glowing on the screen and felt her stomach drop three floors. Mrs Brandt announced, in a voice full of delight, that she was coming for the weekend and that she hoped, above all things, to go with her daughter to hear the orchestra play. Odile heard herself say that this would be lovely, and then she sat down on the floor of the hall with the phone still in her hand.

Sam had heard every word of the call through the thin wall, and he came into the hall with a mug of tea in one hand and a vacuum cleaner in the other. He said, very gently, that he was not offering to fix anything, only to make tea and push a vacuum cleaner, and Odile, who had never once in her life accepted help without an argument, looked at him and nodded. It felt, she thought, like finally laying down a very heavy bag at the end of a long journey.

They cleaned like two people preparing for an inspection, scrubbing the kitchen, polishing the windows and stuffing Sam's cables into every drawer of the study. They argued fiercely about the blue tape, Odile wanting it gone and Sam insisting that it was a respected feature of the flat. In the end, out of sheer weariness, they agreed to leave it where it was and to call it an art project, and the flat had never looked so tidy, or so odd.

On Friday evening Hélène Brandt climbed the four flights of stairs in her best coat, carrying a heavy basket of cheese, plum jam and a cake tin as though they were the crown jewels. She kissed her daughter on both cheeks, held her at arm's length and examined her from head to toe with the expert eye of a mother. Odile, standing very straight, hoped with all her heart that her face gave nothing away.

Odile introduced Sam, in her most casual voice, as her flatmate, a word that seemed to hang in the air for far too long. Her mother shook his hand warmly and, on learning that the flat had only one bedroom, raised her eyebrows with the slow and stately motion of a drawbridge, and she kept them up for some time. Sam, to his great credit, smiled as though he had never in his whole life felt so calm and untroubled.

Sam cooked dinner for three from Dev's most trusted recipe, a slow chicken stew with garlic and herbs, and the whole flat filled with a smell that could have charmed a stone. Mrs Brandt ate two generous plates, tasted the sauce twice with narrowed eyes and finally demanded to know the secret, and Sam, blushing, confessed that it was mostly a friend with a great many opinions. She laughed so heartily at this honest answer that she had to wipe her eyes with a napkin.

While the two of them washed the plates together, Mrs Brandt leaned close and whispered that Sam was absolutely lovely, and that a man who could cook like that should never be allowed to leave. Odile whispered back, rather too quickly, that he was only a flatmate and that it was a temporary arrangement for one month. Her mother only smiled the particular smile that mothers keep for children who protest too much.

That night Mrs Brandt took the bedroom, Odile curled up on the short sofa among the sleeping microphones, and Sam, being the tallest and the most generous, blew up an air bed and laid it in the hall. Its edge touched the famous blue line that neither of them had yet dared to remove. The flat creaked and settled around the three of them, and each of them lay awake for a while, listening to the others breathe.

On Saturday morning, over coffee and plum jam, Mrs Brandt asked brightly which night the orchestra was playing and whether Odile could find them good seats near the front. Odile put down her cup very carefully, as though it were made of glass, and folded her hands in her lap. In a voice she hardly recognised, she said that she had something to tell her, and that she needed her mother to listen to all of it before saying a word.

Odile told her the whole truth, from the afternoon of the audition to the shaking bow, the courteous letter and the long months of hiding it all behind cheerful phone calls. It took a very long time, and her voice wobbled twice and almost broke once, but her mother did not interrupt, and her eyes never left her daughter's face. When it was over, the kitchen was so quiet that they could hear the lemon magnet tick against the fridge.

For a moment Mrs Brandt said nothing at all, and then she rose, came around the table and held her daughter so tightly that the cups on the table rattled. She said that she was proud of everything Odile taught and of every child who left her lessons with a violin under an arm. She reminded her that Grandpa Luc, who had given her that very violin, had played only at weddings and had been the happiest man she ever knew.

On Sunday afternoon Mrs Brandt put on her best coat, kissed her daughter and, to Sam's astonishment, kissed him on both cheeks as well, telling him sternly to keep Odile practising. At the front door she noticed the two keys hanging side by side on one small brass hook. She remarked, with a look of deep satisfaction, that two keys for one door was a strange arrangement but perhaps a good one.

On Monday morning Odile told Sam that she felt lighter than she had in months, as though she had been carrying an invisible suitcase up four flights of stairs and had finally set it down. Then, with a briskness that surprised them both, she offered to help with the choir sessions, since six years of teaching had taught her how to keep forty children from running wild. Sam stared at her in surprise, and then, very slowly, a huge and delighted grin began to spread across his face.

Ms Pereira, the director of the Larkspur Children's Choir, arrived on Tuesday with a clipboard, a silver whistle and an expression that suggested she had seen every kind of rehearsal room in the world. She climbed to the top landing, clapped once, listened for a long moment to the shimmering echo with her head on one side and pronounced that it would do beautifully. Sam let out a breath that he seemed to have been holding for a week.

On Saturday morning forty children in woollen coats and bright scarves arrived and filled the stairwell from the ground floor to the top landing, whispering, giggling, pushing and swapping sweets. Sam darted among them placing microphones on their stands and muttering anxiously to himself like a man defusing a bomb. Ms Pereira stood at the bottom of the stairs with her silver whistle, calm as a lighthouse in a storm, and waited for the chaos to settle.

Odile stepped onto the stairs, raised her hand, and in her gentle teacher's voice showed the children how to stand tall, drop their shoulders and breathe slowly into their stomachs. The giggling thinned, the shuffling stopped, and the long stairwell filled with the soft sound of forty small breaths drawn in together. Ms Pereira looked at her over the clipboard and gave her a short, respectful nod.

The smallest boy in the choir, a gap-toothed child named Arlo, sang the loudest of all and with total confidence a little to the side of every note, and Ms Pereira winced like a woman biting a lemon. Odile knelt beside him on the stair and whispered that the secret of singing was to listen as hard as you sing. Arlo, who had never been asked to listen before, closed his mouth, opened his ears and slowly found the tune.

The first takes all went spectacularly wrong, ruined in turn by a cough, a sneeze, a lorry grinding past in the street and a small girl who suddenly remembered that she had left her gloves in the bus. The last disaster was the best of all, because Biscuit strolled down the stairs through the very middle of the choir with his tail held high. Forty children collapsed into helpless laughter, and Sam, behind the microphone, laughed along with every one of them.

Halfway through the afternoon, when the choir had settled into a gentle lullaby in three parts, the front door of the building banged and Mr Tavish appeared on the lower landing, home early because his sister's boiler had broken. He stood there in his tartan dressing gown with his mouth already open to complain. Then the children's voices rose around him, soft as feathers, and the complaint never came out.

Mr Tavish lowered himself onto a step, folded his arms and listened to the lullaby right to the end, never once making a sound or moving a muscle. When the last note had faded, he cleared his throat, blew his nose loudly in a large checked handkerchief and asked, in a voice rather rougher than before, whether there happened to be a second verse. Ms Pereira said that there was, and the choir sang it just for him.

They recorded the lullaby again in three takes, and the third one, with Mr Tavish glowering contentedly from the second landing and Arlo singing softly in tune, was perfect from the first breath to the last. The children burst into applause that went rolling down the stairwell like a wave, and Sam, peering at Odile over the top of the equipment, held up both his thumbs. She laughed aloud with sheer happiness and held up both of her own thumbs in reply.

On Sunday evening Dev arrived at the top of the stairs panting, beaming and laden with a giant copper pot and four bulging bags of shopping. He announced, to nobody in particular, that he would be cooking a proper dinner for these two starving artists. Then his eyes fell on the blue line running down the hall, and he began to laugh so hard that he had to put the pot down.

Within minutes Dev had taken over the kitchen entirely, giving Sam a knife, an onion and a stream of orders delivered with a wooden spoon. He told Odile in a cheerful stage whisper that her name had come up in his phone conversations with Sam at least forty times that week, and that he had stopped counting at forty. Sam, red to the tips of his ears, chopped his onion with great violence.

At dinner Dev served a feast of spiced rice, roasted vegetables and a lamb stew that fell apart under the spoon, and with every course he produced a more embarrassing story about his oldest friend. The best of them described the afternoon Sam had wept openly over a recording of a whale singing in the deep sea. Odile laughed until the tears ran down her face, and she had to hold on to the table to stay upright.

After the plates had been cleared, Odile took up her violin and played a short, bright dance that set Dev tapping his foot and Biscuit's ears twitching at the window. Dev, sitting back in his chair with his hands folded across his stomach, noticed with deep interest that his friend was not looking at the violin at all but only at the woman playing it. He said nothing at all about it, which for a man like Dev was a truly heroic achievement.

At the sink, while Sam was out of the room searching for a missing cable, Dev dried the dishes beside Odile and spoke in a lower voice than usual. He told her that Sam was the kindest man he had ever met and also the worst in the world at saying what he felt. He had once spent three weeks failing to ask a girl to a concert, he added, and Odile polished the same glass for a very long time without looking up.

At the front door, pulling on his coat, Dev hugged his friend hard and whispered into his ear that he should say it before the month ran out. Sam muttered that he had no idea what Dev meant and that the pot was heavy and he should hurry. Dev only laughed all the way down the four flights of stairs, his big voice booming through the echo like a drum.

On Monday morning the phone rang, and Ms Vane's bright voice announced that she had the most wonderful news. Two separate flats had become free at last, one for each of her unfortunate clients, and she would be delighted to hand over both sets of keys, provided that the top flat was empty and spotless by Sunday. She sounded, from the proud brightness of her voice, as though she fully expected to be thanked for it.

They both said at exactly the same moment that this was great news, wonderful news, the best news in the world, and each of them smiled so brightly that their cheeks ached. Neither of them meant a word of it, and they both knew that the other did not either, which made the whole performance almost unbearable. The line of blue tape ran between them, and for the first time it seemed to be holding something back.

All day they kept to their own corners of the flat like two animals who have sensed bad weather. Sam hunched over his screen behind his closed door and his headphones, working with a fierce and quite unnecessary concentration. Odile played Bach so slowly and so carefully that each note seemed to be set down like a stone in a stream, as if it might be the last she would ever play in this room.

That night they lay awake on either side of the thin wall, each pretending, even to the dark, that they were asleep. At last Odile reached out and tapped twice on the plaster with one knuckle, softly, like a person knocking at a door in a dream. After a long moment of silence two answering taps came back from the other side, and neither of them said anything, and for the first time in days both of them slept.

On Wednesday afternoon Odile's phone buzzed with a long message from Dev, written in capital letters and ending with six exclamation marks. It informed her that tomorrow was Sam's birthday, that Sam had told nobody and intended to spend it working in his study, and that something simply had to be done about it. Odile read it twice, put down her violin and began to make a list.

Odile decided, with the rashness of someone who has never baked a cake in her life, that she would make one herself. She hurried to the shops on Lamplighter Lane to gather her supplies, and she came back up the four flights of stairs with flour, eggs, butter and a lemon. The corner shop had only one packet of birthday candles left, so she bought it, and it held exactly three small candles.

On the morning of his birthday Sam left early for a meeting with Ms Pereira, grumbling about having to wear a shirt, and Odile launched her campaign the moment the door closed behind him. Within half an hour the kitchen looked as if a small snowstorm had broken out in it. Flour covered the counter, the floor and one startled eyebrow, and the oven gave off an ominous, unfamiliar smell.

The cake emerged from the oven leaning to one side like a tired tower, with a deep crater in the middle that no amount of staring could repair. Odile broke off a crumb and tasted it, and her whole face crumpled, because somewhere between the flour and the eggs she had picked up the salt instead of the sugar. It tasted, she thought with a sinking heart, exactly like a mouthful of the sea.

Mrs Okonkwo, who had smelled something peculiar on the stairs, climbed to the top flat with Biscuit under her arm and found Odile sitting among the ruins. She tasted a very small piece of the cake with great courage, swallowed it with equal courage and then remarked, with perfect gravity, that a cake did not have to be good in order to be loved. It only had to be made, she added gently, by someone who cared a great deal about the person who would eat it.

Sam came home early, humming, because his meeting with Ms Pereira had gone far better than he had dared to hope, and he stopped dead in the kitchen doorway. His eyes travelled slowly over the flour on the floor, the flour on the counter, the flour on Odile's eyebrow and the lopsided cake on the table, which wore three small candles like a crooked crown. He opened his mouth, closed it again, and discovered that he had absolutely no idea what to say.

Odile struck a match with trembling fingers, lit the three crooked candles one by one and announced, in a voice that wobbled badly, that the cake was for his birthday and that it was probably awful. Sam looked at the flame, at the cake, and at her, and something shifted in his face that she had never seen there before. He told her that nobody had baked him a cake since he was eight years old.

Sam cut a generous slice, took an enormous bite and chewed it for a very long time with a smile fixed rigidly to his face, while his eyes watered gently from the salt. When he could finally speak, he declared that it was the best cake anyone had ever baked for him, and the astonishing thing was that he seemed to mean it. He ate every crumb of the slice, and then, shamelessly, he asked for another.

To make up for the cake, Odile lifted her violin and played Happy Birthday in the middle of the floury kitchen, slowly and with great tenderness, as though it were a solemn piece by Bach. Sam, sitting on the counter with a second slice in his hand, listened to the old familiar tune turn into something grave and lovely and strange. He found, to his own considerable surprise, that he could not swallow another bite for the lump in his throat.

Sam had no present to give in return, so he went to the study and came back with a small envelope, which he placed in her flour-dusted hand with great solemnity. Inside was a tiny drive labelled in his slanting writing with the words Not Only A Teacher, and it held the very first recording he had made of her on the stairs. She turned it over and over in her fingers, quite speechless, and at last she held it against her chest like a precious stone.

That evening Odile put music on her phone, and before either of them had decided anything at all, they were dancing, clumsily and happily, around the small kitchen with flour still dusting their shoulders. The blue tape ran across the tiles beneath their feet, and each time they stepped over it, they laughed. It was the most foolish and the most perfect hour of the whole month.

In a sudden rush of courage Sam suggested that the tape had done its work and ought to come up, and Odile, after the briefest of pauses, said yes. They knelt on opposite sides of the hall and peeled it off the floorboards inch by inch, meeting in the middle with a ball of blue tape the size of an orange. There was a faint pale line on the wood where it had been, and neither of them mentioned that either, though both of them saw it.

Odile placed the great blue ball solemnly on the kitchen shelf, next to the lemon magnet, and stood back to admire it. She declared, with a perfectly straight face, that it ought to be given to a museum as a record of the strangest treaty ever signed in the city. Sam saluted the ball with great ceremony, and then they both collapsed in helpless laughter against the kitchen cupboards.

That night a great storm swept in over the city, with a sky of purple cloud, a roll of thunder that rattled the windowpanes and rain that fell on the roof of the top flat like handfuls of gravel. Odile lay in bed listening to the drumming on the slates above her head. The wind moaned down the stairwell, and she thought, with the foolish half-sleep logic of the night, that the building was trying to sing.

In the small hours Odile woke to a new sound beneath the rain, a slow and steady plink, plink, plink, which did not belong to the storm. She followed it down the dark hall and into the study and switched on the lamp. A bright thread of water was running down from a crack in the ceiling, straight toward the desk where Sam's hard drive sat among his wires.

On the desk, in the direct path of the water, sat the one small black box that held every note the choir had sung. Odile did not think at all but snatched her coat from the back of the door, flung it over the hard drive like a net over a bird, and shouted for Sam at the very top of her voice. The sound ran down the whole length of the stairwell and came back again in a long and anxious echo.

Sam burst into the study in a tangle of bedclothes, took in the scene in a single horrified glance and gathered the hard drive, the laptop and Winnie into his arms like a father rescuing children from a fire. He carried them down the hall to the highest dry shelf he could find and set them down with trembling hands. Only then, with all the precious things safe at last, did he stop and draw a deep and shaky breath.

They ran to the kitchen, seized every bowl, pan and mixing basin they owned, and set them in a nervous ring beneath the ceiling, where the drips rang like a strange orchestra of tin and china. Sam dialled the emergency number for Vane and Co, and it rang and rang and rang into an empty office. Meanwhile the thunder grumbled on overhead like a creditor at the door, and the rain kept falling.

At the height of the storm there was a hammering at the door, and there stood Mr Tavish in his dressing gown with a ladder over one shoulder and a roll of plastic sheeting under his arm. He announced that he had carried the post through worse weather than this for forty years, and he climbed up to the ceiling with astonishing speed. Within minutes he had sealed the leak with the plastic and a roll of tape, and Odile could have kissed him for it.

When the last drip had ceased and Mr Tavish had gone grumbling back to bed, Odile and Sam sat down side by side on the edge of the bed. The small black hard drive lay on the blanket between them like a sleeping animal, and Sam said quietly that the album was safe, that all forty voices were safe. Odile, to her own astonishment, began to laugh and then, without warning, to cry.

The hug that began as simple relief went on a little longer than a hug of simple relief should. Neither of them moved, and the clock on the wall ticked, and the rain softened to a patter on the repaired roof, and Odile could feel Sam's heart thudding against her shoulder. At last she drew back, said a shy goodnight in a voice that was not her own and walked down the hall without looking round.

At dawn, running on no sleep and a great deal of tea, Sam copied the whole album three times over, onto the laptop and onto a second drive. The third copy went onto a tiny stick that he tucked into a corner of Odile's violin case for safekeeping. It was a ridiculous place for a hiding place and also, as he realised with a start, the safest one he knew, since she would never let that violin out of her sight.

In the morning Ms Vane arrived on the doorstep in a crisp blazer, holding two small envelopes with the pride of a magician who has finally produced the rabbit. Odile's new flat, she announced, was on Harbour Road, and Sam's was on Kiln Street, and she was delighted to say that they were on opposite sides of the city. They were a good hour apart by bus, she added, and nobody in the doorway smiled.

Odile and Sam each took an envelope in silence, and the little paper rectangles felt strangely heavy in their hands. Ms Vane glanced from one stony face to the other, frowned very slightly, looked up at the brown stain on the study ceiling and promised that a roofer would come before the end of the week. She left, her heels clicking down the stairs, a little quicker than she had come.

They spent the rest of the day packing, and they did it without speaking, each working in a separate corner of the flat like people in a library. Sam wrapped and labelled his cables one by one, in his alphabetical order, while Odile folded her clothes into small neat squares and laid them in her suitcase as if she were putting away a dream. The only sounds in the whole flat were the rip of tape and the soft rustle of paper.

Last of all, Odile stood at the fridge and took down the notes one at a time, the sharp ones about socks and the pan and the funny ones with drawings of microphones in moustaches. She smoothed each of them flat on the counter, folded it and laid it in the lid of her violin case, together with the lemon magnet and the timetable. She did not stop to ask herself why a person would keep such things, and she did not want to know the answer.

By evening the flat that had been so crowded and noisy and alive had been stripped down to bare floors and bare walls, and every footstep rang out through it with a hollow, lonely echo. The rooms seemed to know that the two strangers who had quarrelled in them, laughed in them and mended each other in them were going. The sound of the empty hall, the long thin sound of a single door closing, was like a sigh.

That evening Mrs Okonkwo invited Odile down for tea, poured it strong and sweet and, after a few minutes of ordinary conversation, set down her cup. She announced that she had made up her mind at last, and that she was going to move to the sea to live near Ngozi at the end of the month. Biscuit would go with her in a wicker basket, she added, and would complain loudly all the way.

Then she looked over the rim of her cup with her sharpest look and told Odile that she and that young man upstairs were the two most foolish people she had ever had the pleasure of knowing. They were quiet as mice, she said, and blind as moles, and a mouse and a mole could sit on one cheese for a year and never notice they were hungry for the same thing. Odile opened her mouth to protest and found, to her dismay, that she had no words at all.

Odile climbed the four flights slowly, and at the top she stopped, because the door of the empty study was ajar and Sam's low voice was coming through it. He was talking quietly to Winnie, the way a man talks when he thinks nobody is listening, and he said that he did not want to go, not to Kiln Street, not anywhere. She stood in the dark hall without moving, and her heart began to pound so loudly that she was afraid he would hear it.

Dev met Sam the next morning at a small café on the corner and, without a word of greeting, pushed a plate of lemon cake across the table toward him. He told him, with unusual solemnity, that a man who could record forty children for four weeks without panicking could surely say a few true words to one woman, and that he must do it before it was too late. Sam stared down at the cake as if it might offer him some advice.

Sam shook his head and said that Odile had her violin and a bright future that she was only now beginning to believe in. All he had to offer, he said, was a heap of cables and a studio that he could not afford. Dev replied, with heartfelt contempt, that it was the silliest speech he had heard in thirty years, but Sam was not yet ready to be convinced.

At her last lesson before Saturday's recital, Tilly stood in the empty front room with her violin under her chin, and her small hands shook so badly that the bow chattered on the strings. She whispered, in a very small voice, that she was terribly afraid she would freeze on the stage in front of everybody. The words went through Odile like a cold draught, because she knew exactly what that felt like.

Odile knelt on the floor in front of the girl and did not offer her a comforting lie. She told her honestly that her own arm had once shaken so badly that she had had to stop playing, and that the feeling had passed in the end. The first thing to do, she said, was to breathe slowly and to look for the face of one friend in the room, and she promised to be that friend in the very front row.

Sam, who had been standing at the door pretending to read a label, quietly offered to record Tilly's piece and put the headphones on her head when the take was over. She listened with a frown, and then a look of amazement crept over her face, because the girl on the recording played steadily and sweetly and without a single shake. It was the first time she had ever heard herself the way other people did.

On the last night before the deadline they sat side by side at the laptop and finished the mix together, passing a single pair of headphones back and forth like a pair of conspirators. When the final song was balanced to his satisfaction, Sam asked, rather shyly, whether Odile's violin might open the very first track of the album. He meant a single long note from the stairwell, and she said yes before he had even finished asking.

On Friday morning Sam sat in front of the laptop with the finished album attached to an email, and his finger hovered over the send button as if it were a hot coal. At last Odile laid her hand over his, and together, with a small click, they sent forty children's voices and one violin out into the world. For a long moment the whole room seemed to take one deep breath in and to forget how to let it out.

Within an hour Ms Pereira had replied, but her message contained only a few brisk words, thanking him and promising to say more soon, and it told them nothing whatever. Sam spent the entire afternoon pretending that he was not waiting for anything, tidying cables that were already tidy and glancing at the silent phone every ninety seconds. Odile pretended not to notice, with great and tactful kindness, and quietly brought him a mug of tea at four.

That evening Odile played through Tilly's little piece over and over, so that every phrase of it would be in her fingers and her heart and she could play it in her sleep if she were needed. Sam sat on the floor of the hall with his back to the wall and listened. He promised that he would be at the Corn Hall tomorrow with a microphone, to record the recital for Tilly's family and to make sure that, whatever happened, it would be kept.

That night neither of them slept, and each of them knew it, because the old pipes had never been so quiet and the walls had never been so thin. Odile lay staring at the pale ceiling, listening to the small creaks of a man turning over on the far side of the plaster. After a long time there came one single soft tap on the wall, and then another, and she answered it, and lay smiling in the dark.

On Saturday morning Tilly stood outside the Corn Hall in a new blue dress, flanked by her parents like a small and anxious queen between two guards. When Odile took her hand to say hello, it was as cold as a stone from the river. The girl gave her a quick, brave smile that was almost more painful to see than tears.

In a small side room smelling of dust and rosin, Odile tied a blue ribbon in Tilly's hair, straightened the girl's collar and knelt to look her in the eye. She promised to sit in the very front row, right in the middle, and told Tilly that whenever she felt afraid she must look at her and nobody else. Tilly nodded, solemn as a judge, and clutched her violin a little tighter against her chest.

The Corn Hall slowly filled with parents, grandparents and fidgeting children in their best clothes, and the noise of two hundred voices rose to the rafters like a flock of starlings. At the very back, Sam set up a microphone on a stand and checked his levels with a frown. Beside him sat Dev, Mrs Okonkwo and Mr Tavish, who had been invited and who had arrived wearing a tie and an expression of fierce neutrality.

The recital began with a boy who beat a drum with tremendous enthusiasm and no sense of rhythm, followed by two sisters with recorders who squeaked their way through a folk tune. After them came a very serious girl who played a slow piece on a cello that was nearly as big as she was. The hall clapped warmly for every one of them, and in the front row Odile found that she was gripping her programme so hard that it had begun to tear.

At last the announcer called out the name Tilly Marsh, and a small figure in a blue dress walked across the wide wooden stage toward the middle, looking smaller with every step in the glare of the lights. She stopped at last in the very centre of the stage and searched the dark rows until she found Odile's face. She lifted her violin to her chin, and the entire hall seemed to lean forward with her.

She began beautifully, with a clear sweet tone, and played the first eight bars without a flaw. Then, as though a hidden door had slammed somewhere in her head, the next note vanished completely. Her bow stopped in mid-air, her face went white, and the hall fell so silent that Odile could hear the clock above the door and the sound of a hundred people holding their breath.

In the front row Odile remembered with terrible clarity the dark hall, the scratching pencil and her own arm shaking like a leaf. She knew exactly how cold, how heavy and how endless that kind of silence felt from the inside. A voice in her head, which sounded oddly like Sam's, told her that a chair was not a violin, and without deciding anything at all, she stood up from her seat.

Odile lifted her own violin from its case under the seat, walked up the five wooden steps onto the stage and crossed the boards in front of two hundred astonished faces. She stood at Tilly's side, so close that their shoulders touched, and she lifted her bow like a person about to cross a river. She did not look at the audience even once, because the only person who mattered in the whole hall was nine years old and trembling.

Odile whispered the single word breathe, lifted her bow and played the opening bars of the piece very softly, like a gentle hand held out in the dark. Tilly's bow trembled, then came down, and the tune came flooding back into her fingers. The two violins went on together, one steady and one shining, until the girl's small sound grew bright enough to stand on its own.

Little by little Odile let her own sound fade away, a ribbon of music being gently untied from a package, until only Tilly's violin was left in the great hall. The girl played on alone in the great and hushed hall, with her chin held high and her eyes shining. She drew out the final note so steadily that the hall seemed to hold it in its hands, and not a single shake touched her bow from beginning to end.

The hall erupted into applause that shook the dust from the old rafters, and one by one the audience rose to their feet until the whole room was a sea of clapping hands. Tilly made a deep and serious bow, then dropped all her dignity and ran across the stage. She flung her arms around Odile's waist, and Odile held her, laughing and crying at once.

At the back of the hall Sam wiped his eyes on his sleeve, pressed the stop button with a shaking thumb and found that he could not speak at all. Beside him Mr Tavish blew his nose with a sound like a trumpet, folded his handkerchief and observed gruffly that it had not been bad, for people who had learned their trade on a staircase. Mrs Okonkwo smiled quietly to herself in the next seat, while Dev, with no shame at all, openly sobbed into his scarf.

In a quiet side room, while the crowd was still murmuring in the hall, Odile sat down on a stool and looked at her right hand, which lay in her lap as calm as a sleeping bird. She had played in front of two hundred people, with no preparation, no rehearsal and no thought of herself. Her arm had not trembled once, and the discovery made her feel dizzy with a kind of silent joy.

That evening, as the street lamps blinked into life one after another along Lamplighter Lane, Odile and Sam walked home together through the soft blue dusk. Sam carried the microphone stand over his shoulder like a fishing rod, and Odile carried her violin. They walked so slowly that the lamps seemed to be lighting themselves just for them.

Under the lamp outside number 22, with the whole tall house leaning over them in the dusk, Odile stopped walking and told him that she dreaded the move. She said that she had not known that one month, one coin and one strip of blue tape could change a life. Nothing else she had ever known, she told him, had sounded like this flat, with its pipes and its echoes and its two keys.

Sam looked at the pavement, then at the lamp, then, with a visible effort, at her face, and said that he was very bad at saying things. Then he said that he did not want to move either, not to Kiln Street and not to any other street in the world. He did not want to go anywhere at all if she were not going to be there, and it all came out in a rush, and he looked astonished.

Then he reached into his coat pocket and drew out a folded letter, which he held up in the lamplight with a hand that shook slightly. He explained that he had written to the landlord, Mr Quill, a week ago, and that Mr Quill had just come home from abroad and replied. Mrs Okonkwo's flat on the third floor would be free to let at the end of the month, the letter said, to anyone who could prove that they loved the building.

Odile laughed out loud with sheer surprise, a clear bright sound that rang down the empty lane. Then she lifted her chin and asked, with her eyebrow raised in the old familiar way, whether he was asking her to move into the flat downstairs as a flatmate or as something more. The whole street seemed to wait for his answer, and so did the lamp, which flickered.

Sam answered in a voice barely above a whisper that he meant more, a great deal more, and Odile said yes before he had even finished the word. They climbed the four flights of stairs hand in hand, and on the top landing, beneath the round window with the moon sailing in it, they kissed. The stairwell, which had kept so many secrets, sang the sound of it softly up and down.

From somewhere far below came the soft click of a door opening a crack on the third floor, and then the voice of Mrs Okonkwo, floating up the stairwell with perfect calm, remarking that it was high time. A grey tail swished once, twice, in the narrow gap of the doorway, and then it was gone. The door closed again with a small, satisfied snap, as though the old woman had just won a bet with herself.

Long after midnight they sat at the kitchen table, among the packed boxes, and drew a plan of Flat 3B on the back of an old envelope. It had two bedrooms, a great sunlit front room, tall windows and a dusty piano, and for once there was nothing at all to argue about, so that not a single coin had to be tossed. They looked at the drawing and then at each other and burst out laughing.

On Sunday morning a knock sounded at the door of 4B, and when Sam opened it, a tall, sun-browned man in a tweed coat was standing on the mat with a battered suitcase at his feet. He introduced himself as Mr Quill, the landlord, just that moment landed from abroad. He apologised at once and most sincerely for the double booking, which he blamed on his agent's computer and, he added with a sigh, on his own long absence.

Mrs Okonkwo, in her best cardigan, opened the door of Flat 3B and led them through the rooms with the dignity of a duchess showing off her castle. Mr Quill walked slowly through the big sunlit front room, gazing up at the high ceilings. He said with feeling that the echo in this building was the finest in the city, a fact that had been in his family for three generations.

Mr Quill produced a lease from his case, laid it on the piano and asked them, with great seriousness, whether they were quite sure. A lease with two names on one page, he said, was in its own way a promise. Odile and Sam looked at each other across the dusty lid of the piano, and the whole month seemed to pass between them in a single glance, and they both said yes at exactly the same moment.

Odile rang Ms Vane on speaker and cancelled the two flats on Harbour Road and Kiln Street, and there was a short, stunned silence on the line. Then Ms Vane said, in a voice of pure happiness, that she was delighted beyond words and that she would tear up two files at once. Her computer, which had been in disgrace for weeks, was almost certainly delighted too.

Sam rang Dev to tell him everything, and the first thing that came out of the phone was a shout so loud that Sam had to hold it at arm's length while the whole kitchen vibrated. When the noise had settled, Dev insisted that he had known it all along, from the very first week. He expected, he said, to be best man at the wedding, a remark that made Odile blush and made Sam say nothing at all.

Odile telephoned her mother with the news and heard a shriek of joy at the other end of the line that nearly made her drop the phone. Mrs Brandt cried that she had known it from the moment she saw those two keys hanging on one hook, and she promised to come very soon with a basket of plum jam and cheese. Then she asked, in a quieter voice, whether Odile was happy, and Odile said that she was, more than she could say.

Then, in the middle of the dust and the boxes, Sam's phone rang with Ms Pereira's name on the screen, and he answered it with a face the colour of paper. She told him in her brisk way that the choir adored the album and that the children had cried when they heard themselves. A respected record company wanted to release it in the autumn and would pay him properly for his work, she added, and she would like Odile to become the choir's violin teacher.

Sam ended the call, slid slowly down the wall until he was sitting on the bare floorboards, and whispered, to nobody in particular, that his studio was safe. All the weeks of dread seemed to leave him at once, like air out of a balloon. Odile sat beside him, took his hand and said nothing, because she knew better than anyone that there are moments when the kindest words are no words at all.

Mrs Okonkwo patted the lid of the old piano as one pats the head of a faithful dog and told them that it would not be going to the sea. It detested salt air, she said, and had never once behaved well on a journey. It would stay where it belonged, in the front room of Flat 3B, and she hoped that someone would at last play it again, and she looked at Odile and Sam with great meaning.

On moving day Sam and Odile carried their boxes down a single flight of stairs, which, after weeks of climbing four, felt like the shortest journey in the world. Dev puffed after them with the heaviest crates, and Mr Tavish held the doors and issued orders. Biscuit sat on the middle step with his tail curled round his paws, supervising the whole enterprise with an expression of mild disapproval.

When the last box had gone, Odile climbed back up for a final look at the empty flat that had held so much. She knelt in the hall and touched with one finger the faint pale line on the floorboards where the blue tape had once run. Sam came and stood behind her, and without a word his hand found hers, and the rooms around them sighed with the satisfaction of a house that has done its work.

A taxi drew up at the kerb to take Mrs Okonkwo to the station and the sea, and she hugged Odile and Sam in turn, hard and long, and told them to mind the echo. At that moment Biscuit burst from his wicker basket like a grey rocket and tore up the steps and into the hall. Mrs Okonkwo, after one long look at the empty doorway, laughed and said that he had made his choice and that they must look after him.

Mr Quill met them on the third-floor landing in his tweed coat, with the afternoon sun making a golden mist of the dust in the stairwell, and he held out a brass ring with two new keys on it. He placed the ring gently in their joined hands, as one might hand over a very small and valuable bird. He remarked, with a perfectly straight face, that this time there had been no mistake whatever, since the lease had been written by a human being and checked twice.

Each of them took one key from the ring, and at exactly the same moment they pushed them into the lock of Flat 3B, which was a thing that nobody else in the world would ever have thought of doing. Both keys turned, with the same smooth, satisfied click that had once alarmed them so much on the fourth floor. The door swung slowly open onto a sunlit room that smelled of old wood and tea.

Inside the big front room, the afternoon sun lay in long gold bars across the bare floor, and the old piano waited by the wall with its lid half open. The high ceiling hummed with a faint echo of everything that had ever been said there. They stood side by side without moving, taking in the room, and it came to them both that there was not a single line to draw, and not a single thing that needed dividing.

That evening, while the boxes still stood in tottering towers around the kitchen, Odile fixed the old lemon magnet to the door of the new fridge and wrote the first note of their new home in her neat upright capitals. It asked, quite simply and without the smallest flourish, whether there might possibly be soup for supper. When she returned from the bedroom, she found that Sam had added underneath it, in his hurried slanting hand, a small drawing of a bowl wearing a splendid moustache.

As the leaves turned, Odile taught violin to the choir children every Tuesday and played in a small quartet at weddings across the city, as Grandpa Luc had once done. She found, to her quiet and lasting joy, that her right arm obeyed her again without a single tremor. Sam's little studio, which had been so close to failing, filled up with bands, podcasters and an elderly poet, and its busy door seemed to open and close all day.

On the night of the album launch the Corn Hall was full to the doors, and the Larkspur Children's Choir filed onto the stage in their scarves and sang the lullaby that had begun it all. Little Arlo sang in tune at last, and Tilly played a short solo in a blue dress. In the front row Mr Tavish, wearing his best tie and a look of private pride, wept without the slightest shame.

Months later the choir album was sold in shops across the country, and the very first track began with a single, shimmering note from Odile's violin. That evening she and Sam climbed the steps of Lamplighter Lane together, each with a key in hand, and opened the same door at the same moment. Inside, the lamp was already lit, the cat was already asleep and the sound of home was waiting.
